harder.updated_question: Big 5 personality traits of EFL teachers
harder.verification_criterion: The answer identifies all five dimensions of the Big Five personality model (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism) in the context of EFL (English as a Foreign Language) teachers.

attempts.answer:
# Overview: Big Five personality in EFL/ESL teacher contexts

The Big Five model—openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism/emotional stability—has been applied to English as a Foreign/Second Language (EFL/ESL) teachers and trainees to understand how relatively stable individual differences relate to classroom behaviors, reflective practice, emotional regulation, and student outcomes.<cite id="0c139ee0-4">The Big Five framework has been widely adopted in organizational and applied research because it is valid, parsimonious, and supported by strong evidence, and it conceptualizes personality as relatively stable patterns of cognition, affect, and behavior</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-1">Big Five traits have been linked to reflective teaching among Iranian EFL teachers, motivating empirical work on trait–practice associations in EFL</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-4">Reviews of successful ESL/EFL teachers identify a set of characteristic strengths that map onto interpersonal, self-regulatory, and openness-related dispositions</cite>. Across studies, extraversion, conscientiousness, and neuroticism frequently emerge as strongest for day-to-day classroom processes and student interactions, whereas openness and agreeableness show more nuanced or indirect relationships to core EFL pedagogy, depending on context and outcome.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism are closely tied to EFL processes and outcomes; extraversion supports participation and oral development, conscientiousness supports organization and self-control for learning tasks, and neuroticism relates to anxiety that can hinder engagement</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-1">Openness and agreeableness are less directly tied to core EFL tasks that require sustained effort (e.g., vocabulary, reading), with weaker or inconsistent associations to EFL effectiveness</cite>.

# How Big Five has been measured in EFL/ESL

EFL/ESL studies commonly use validated Big Five instruments (e.g., BFI; NEO-based short forms) adapted for local populations, with robust internal consistency and convergent validity.<cite id="0c139ee0-0">The Big Five Inventory (BFI) has been adapted for EFL learners to assess the five domains (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness) using 44–46 items on a 5-point Likert scale</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-2">BFI domains (8–10 items) show acceptable internal consistency (e.g., α≈0.62–0.83 overall; openness α≈0.75), supporting its use for prospective teachers</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">A shortened Chinese NEO-based Big Five for university teachers (35 items) shows high internal consistency (α≈0.81–0.90) and structural validity, with all dimensions loading well</cite>. In teacher education settings, Big Five assessments have been paired with measures of pedagogical skills or reflective practice to model teacher development and selection-relevant profiles.<cite id="0c139ee0-3">Among 277 Malaysian TESL trainees, Big Five profiles were linked to verbal communication skills, a core pedagogical competence</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-1">Studies in Iranian EFL teacher cohorts explicitly test relationships between Big Five traits and reflective teaching quality</cite>.

# Trait-by-trait evidence in EFL/ESL contexts

Openness to experience. In EFL/ESL trainees, openness shows the clearest positive linkage to verbal/linguistic communication behaviors, suggesting value for fostering interactive language use and creativity in EFL classes.<cite id="0c139ee0-3">Only openness among Big Five traits positively related to verbal communication skills in Malaysian TESL trainees, warranting emphasis to maximize effective communication</cite>. In Chinese university teacher samples, openness is measured reliably and theoretically tied to receptivity to novel ideas and tasks; however, some EFL learner-focused work argues that openness contributes less directly to core EFL effectiveness than self-regulatory and sociable traits.<cite id="f67e7d50-0">Big Five dimensions (including openness) exhibit strong psychometric structure in Chinese university teachers</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-1">Openness is more strongly associated with creativity-oriented domains than with sustained effort tasks central to EFL learning</cite>.

Conscientiousness. Conscientious teachers tend to be more organized, disciplined, and goal-directed, which maps onto lesson planning, materials management, and independent learner support—key to EFL effectiveness.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness is characterized by goal orientation and self-discipline, aligning with systematic study practices (e.g., vocabulary memorization, grammar note-taking) that directly enhance language outcomes</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Prior EFL work indicates teachers’ affective/surgency and personality factors (including conscientious traits) impact students’ achievement and motivation</cite>. Among EFL/ESL instructors, conscientiousness is repeatedly implicated in student attainment and classroom organization, reinforcing its salience for EFL contexts.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Studies report extroversion and friendliness contribute to student success, and broader EFL evidence links teachers’ affective factors to attainment</cite>.

Extraversion. Extraversion (surgency/affectivity) is consistently linked to classroom rapport, participation, and management, which are critical in communicative EFL classes.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">EFL/ESL studies emphasize the effectiveness of teachers’ extroversion and friendliness for students’ success, especially with adult learners</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">A comparative study of extroverted vs. introverted EFL teachers in Iran found extroverted teachers reported more proficient class management and students perceived content more positively and showed greater motivation</cite>. Direct EFL teacher evidence also shows strong positive correlations between overall Big Five profiles and classroom management quality, with extraversion contributing to lively, inspirational environments.<cite id="4f2bf94b-0">A quantitative study of Palestinian EFL teachers found strong positive correlations between Big Five traits and effective classroom management practices</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Well-adjusted emotional and affective personality helps teachers develop lively and inspirational EFL learning environments</cite>.

Agreeableness. Agreeableness aligns with empathy, cooperation, and interpersonal harmony, supporting student–teacher rapport and collaborative learning; however, direct links to core EFL task performance are often weaker or indirect compared to conscientiousness and extraversion.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Agreeableness (empathy/cooperation) may be less directly tied to core EFL tasks that rely on individual effort, with weaker or inconsistent links to EFL effectiveness</cite>. Teacher-education studies that include reflective practice emphasize that agreeableness can shape how teachers engage peers and mediate conflicts, which indirectly supports EFL classroom climate.<cite id="0c139ee0-1">Big Five traits, including agreeableness, relate to reflective teaching, affecting how teachers interact and problem-solve in EFL contexts</cite>.

Neuroticism (low emotional stability). Higher neuroticism is associated with anxiety and self-doubt that can undermine engagement and persistence; in teacher contexts, it tends to correlate negatively with effective classroom processes, whereas lower neuroticism supports emotional regulation and calm instruction.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Neurotic learners (and by extension neurotic teachers) are prone to anxiety and self-doubt, which can hinder engagement and persistence in EFL tasks</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Teachers’ positive personality traits and wellbeing correlate with effective practices; in contrast, no association with stressors highlights the role of adaptive regulation</cite>. Emotional self-regulation research shows that teachers with stronger regulation report fewer behavioral conflicts and stronger student–teacher bonds, consistent with lower trait neuroticism supporting classroom processes.<cite id="7065a9a1-2">Teachers with stronger self-regulation and empathy reported fewer behavioral conflicts, improved communication, and stronger emotional bonds with students</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-3">Emotional intelligence was positively associated with classroom management, learning environment, instruction, and relationships; social skills and empathy showed the strongest correlations</cite>.

Mechanisms: emotional regulation and affective climate
Multiple EFL studies indicate that personality-linked affectivity and surgency interact with emotional regulation to shape classroom dynamics and student outcomes.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Personality-linked extroversion and friendliness contribute to students’ success; extraversion fosters lively, inspirational environments</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extraversion/introversion differences yielded significant differences in class management and student motivation in EFL settings</cite>. In Chinese university EFL contexts, Big Five measures have been used to model how openness, conscientiousness, and agreeableness interplay with emotion regulation to affect classroom engagement, suggesting that self-regulation mediates trait–outcome links.<cite id="f67e7d50-0">A Big Five–based model of Chinese university teachers linked teacher personality to students’ classroom engagement with a mediating role of emotional regulation</cite>. Broad teacher research shows that emotional intelligence—self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, social skills—correlates with and improves classroom processes (management, relationships, learning environment), providing a plausible pathway from Big Five (especially conscientiousness and extraversion; lower neuroticism) to effective EFL practice.<cite id="7065a9a1-3">Emotional intelligence was positively associated with effective classroom processes (management, relationships, learning environment, instruction)</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-2">Higher emotional intelligence supported fewer conflicts and stronger bonds, consistent with emotionally intelligent teachers creating prosocial learning environments</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-0">Emotional intelligence significantly predicted teachers’ conflict management (β≈0.49, R²≈0.24), supporting mediation pathways from affective traits to classroom effectiveness</cite>.

# Cross-cultural patterns and contextual moderators

Across cultures, the Big Five–to–teaching effectiveness link is robust, but the relative salience of traits can shift with educational norms and classroom demands. In Palestinian EFL schools, overall Big Five strongly correlates with classroom management, highlighting generalizability of the pattern.<cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Big Five traits showed a strong positive correlation with effective classroom management among Palestinian EFL teachers</cite>. In Iran, EFL teacher studies tie Big Five to reflective practice and show extroverted teachers manage classes more proficiently and motivate students better, aligning with extraversion’s role in interactive pedagogy.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extroverted EFL teachers reported more proficient class management; students in extroverted teachers’ classes perceived content better and were more motivated</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-1">Big Five traits relate to reflective teaching among Iranian EFL teachers</cite>. In Malaysia, only openness among trainee teachers correlated positively with verbal communication, pointing to culture- and curriculum-specific emphases (e.g., communicative competence in EFL).<cite id="0c139ee0-3">Only openness positively related to verbal communication among Malaysian TESL trainees, recommending greater attention to communication skills</cite>. In China, both psychometric validity and conceptual analyses indicate conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism are most consequential for EFL processes and outcomes, with openness and agreeableness less directly tied to core tasks; conversely, Big Five profiles have been modeled as affecting classroom engagement through emotional regulation.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism are closely related to EFL processes and effectiveness; openness and agreeableness show weaker or inconsistent associations</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">Chinese university teachers’ Big Five shows strong structural validity and links to student engagement via emotional regulation</cite>. These patterns align with cross-disciplinary findings that extraversion and conscientiousness generally predict teacher effectiveness and student engagement, while emotional stability moderates stress and burnout risks in demanding educational settings.<cite id="7065a9a1-2">Emotion regulation strategies help teachers maintain composure and effectiveness amid high emotional demands</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-4">Emotional intelligence accounts for substantial variance in discipline strategies and supports behavior management and overall success</cite>.

# Practical implications for EFL teacher selection, development, and research

- Selection and profiling: Prioritize conscientiousness, extraversion, openness to experience, and lower neuroticism as initial markers for EFL teacher candidates, with attention to openness when programs emphasize creativity and content-creation. Validate locally using adapted BFI/NEO instruments with demonstrated reliability and cultural fit.<cite id="0c139ee0-0">BFI provides established psychometric coverage for EFL populations</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">NEO-based Chinese Big Five shows strong reliability and validity for university teachers</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Big Five correlates positively with classroom management in EFL teaching settings</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-3">Openness uniquely predicted verbal communication skills among TESL trainees</cite>.
- Developmental levers: Target emotional intelligence and self-regulation training to amplify the effects of core traits—improving classroom climate, behavior management, and rapport—especially for introverted or neurotic teachers seeking to build energizing, organized classes.<cite id="7065a9a1-3">Emotional intelligence training improved teachers’ interpersonal competencies and classroom processes</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-0">Emotional intelligence significantly predicted conflict management among teachers</cite>.
- Cultural tailoring: In cultures emphasizing rote learning and compliance, strengthen conscientiousness and emotional stability; in communicative, interaction-focused EFL programs, emphasize extraversion, openness, and reflective practice to foster participation and motivation.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness and extraversion map onto concrete EFL task effectiveness</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extroversion and friendliness boost student success, with extroverted EFL teachers managing classes more effectively</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-3">Openness uniquely linked to verbal communication in Malaysian trainees</cite>.
- Measurement and fairness: Use locally validated instruments and triangulate personality with classroom observations and student outcomes to avoid overreliance on self-report and to align traits with EFL-specific competencies (e.g., speaking interaction, writing feedback, materials organization).<cite id="f67e7d50-0">Local adaptation of Big Five maintains psychometric integrity and supports culture-specific modeling</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Quantitative links between Big Five and classroom management provide outcome-relevant validation</cite>.

# Limitations and open questions

Evidence is strongest for associations—correlations and quasi-experimental contrasts—rather than causal effects; mediation via emotion regulation is plausible but needs more EFL-specific longitudinal studies. Trait salience may vary by school type (public vs. private), learner age, and proficiency level; more cross-cultural meta-analyses focused on EFL teacher cohorts would clarify effect sizes and moderators. Finally, agreeableness and openness may matter more for collegial and curriculum contexts (e.g., team teaching, project-based EFL) where individual task persistence is less central, but direct EFL outcome evidence remains mixed.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Openness and agreeableness may be less directly tied to core EFL task effectiveness, though they can influence creativity-oriented domains</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-4">Despite widespread use of Big Five, there remains a paucity of studies directly linking Big Five traits to reflective teaching in EFL, calling for more applied research</cite>.

# Bottom line: Big Five traits that tend to characterize effective EFL teachers

- Extraversion: energizes interaction, rapport, and classroom management; linked to higher student motivation and positive perception in EFL settings.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extroverted teachers reported more proficient class management; students in extroverted teachers’ classes were more motivated and had better perception</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Big Five strongly correlates with effective classroom management in Palestinian EFL teachers</cite>.
- Conscientiousness: supports organization, planning, and disciplined instruction; directly tied to language-learning routines and student attainment patterns in EFL.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness promotes goal-directed, self-disciplined study behaviors that enhance language outcomes</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Teachers’ affective/surgency and personality factors contribute to student success</cite>.
- Openness to experience: fosters creativity, receptivity to novel content, and communicative fluency; especially relevant for interactive and creative EFL tasks and teacher–trainee communication.<cite id="0c139ee0-3">Openness uniquely predicted verbal communication skills among EFL/ESL trainees</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">Openness shows strong structural validity in Chinese university teachers</cite>.
- Agreeableness: aids empathy, collaboration, and conflict resolution, indirectly supporting EFL climate and participation; direct links to core task performance are weaker or inconsistent.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Agreeableness is less directly tied to core EFL tasks; shows weaker or inconsistent associations with EFL effectiveness</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-1">Big Five relates to reflective teaching, which often involves empathic, collaborative stances</cite>.
- Emotional stability (low neuroticism): reduces anxiety and emotional volatility, enabling calm, consistent instruction and better behavior management; higher neuroticism is associated with challenges in persistence and classroom composure.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Neurotic learners are prone to anxiety and self-doubt, hindering EFL engagement; by extension, higher neuroticism can undermine teacher effectiveness</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-2">Self-regulation and empathy reduce conflicts and build stronger student–teacher bonds</cite>.

Taken together, effective EFL teachers typically exhibit high extraversion and conscientiousness, openness to experience aligned with program goals, agreeableness for collaborative climate, and low neuroticism supported by strong emotional regulation, with implementation details shifting across cultures and curricula.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extraversion and conscientiousness are repeatedly linked to EFL classroom effectiveness and student outcomes</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">Chinese university teacher Big Five modeling shows openness, conscientiousness, and agreeableness structure and links to engagement via regulation</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-3">Openness uniquely supports verbal communication in EFL/ESL trainee samples</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Overall Big Five correlates strongly with classroom management among EFL teachers</cite>.

Title: The Impact of Teachers’ Personality on Senior High School EFL Learners’ General English Achievement
Snippet: This study is primarily designed to discover the effect of teachers' personality on the EFL learners' general English achievement at the pre-intermediate level. A study of this kind can possibly uncover valuable information to aid teachers in improving their personality to enhance the students' general English achievement. The objective of this study is to examine the impact of teachers' personality on senior high school EFL learners' general English achievement. Moreover, the objective of this study was also to examine how the teachers' personality can influence their teaching effectiveness. 

The study may be significant if it directly deals with helping teachers to recognize the importance of their personality role in enhancing students' achievement and general English achievement. Title: The mediating role of emotion regulation in the link between personality traits and self-regulated learning among low-achieving EFL learners
Snippet: To explore personality traits, this study adopts the Five-Factor Model of Personality (FFM), given its wide validation in conceptualizing personality in the field of education 18 . The full spectrum of the FFM comprises five traits: conscientiousness (featured by goal orientation and self-discipline), openness to experience (featured by curiosity and imagination), extraversion (featured by sociability), agreeableness (featured by empathy and cooperation), and neuroticism (featured by emotional instability). Specifically, this study focuses on conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism but excludes openness and agreeableness for three reasons. First, conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism are closely related to the EFL learning process and its effectiveness. For instance, conscientious learners, with strong organisation and self-control, often engage in systematic practices like vocabulary memorisation and grammar note-taking, which can directly enhance language outcomes 5 . Extraverted students, who are usually more outgoing and social, are more inclined to participate in speaking activities and thus support oral English development 5 . In contrast, neurotic learners, prone to anxiety and self-doubt, may struggle with engagement and persistence in the demanding process of EFL learning 19 . Second, prior research has identified these three traits as significant predictors of EFL performance 5,20 . Third, openness to experience and agreeableness are less relevant to core EFL learning tasks. Specifically, openness to experience, which emphasises imagination and novelty, is more strongly associated with creativity-oriented domains such as art or literature 21 , rather than with the sustained effort and persistence required in EFL learning. Similarly, agreeableness, which reflects interpersonal harmony, appears to be less directly relevant to core EFL tasks that rely heavily on individual efforts (e.g., vocabulary acquisition and reading comprehension). Also, empirical studies have also suggested that openness and agreeableness demonstrate weaker or inconsistent associations with EFL effectiveness 5 . Given these considerations, the present study focuses on exploring conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism as the key personality traits influencing the EFL learning process.
</snippet>

Title: Effects of Emotional Intelligence on Conflict Management (Survey of Secondary School Teachers in Dera Ismail Khan, Pakistan)
Snippet: Emotional intelligence (EI) has emerged as a critical determinant of effective interpersonal behavior within educational institutions. Teachers who understand, regulate, and utilize emotions constructively can transform classroom conflicts into opportunities for collaboration and growth. This study aimed to assess the relationship between emotional intelligence and conflict-management abilities among secondary-school teachers in Dera Ismail Khan, Pakistan, while examining gender- and experience-based variations. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was adopted. Data were collected from 300 teachers using the Emotional Intelligence Scale for Teachers (Dey & Ratan, 2022) and Rahim’s Organizational Conflict Inventory–II Form B (Rahim, 2002). Reliability values were satisfactory (α = 0.831 for EI; α = 0.885 for conflict management). Pearson’s correlation (r = 0.492, p < 0.001) showed a significant positive association between EI and conflict management. Regression analysis confirmed that EI significantly predicted conflict management (β = 0.492, R² = 0.242). Female teachers scored higher on emotional intelligence, while male teachers exhibited stronger conflict-management skills (p < 0.001). ANOVA revealed significant differences across age, qualification, and service length (p ≤ 0.05). The findings suggest that emotionally competent teachers are better equipped to resolve interpersonal disputes and create positive learning environments. These results align with organizational behavior research showing that emotional regulation reduces resource depletion and enhances productivity (Javeed & Siddique, 2024). Integrating EI training into teacher development programs is recommended to enhance conflict resolution skills and overall institutional harmony. These results reinforce the role of emotional regulation in organizational behavior and align with recent findings linking psychological resources and workplace effectiveness (Javeed & Siddique, 2025).
</snippet>

Title: Psychological features of emotional relationships in primary school teachers
Snippet: The results of this study reveal the complex and multifaceted nature of emotional relationships within primary school teachers' professional experiences. The findings underscore that emotional intelligence, especially components such as self-regulation, empathy, and emotional awareness, plays a crucial role in determining the quality and stability of teacher-student relationships. Teachers who demonstrate strong emotional control and empathy can create supportive, trusting, and productive learning environments. These results are consistent with the theoretical perspectives of Goleman (2005) and Salovey and Sluyter (1997), who emphasized that individuals with high emotional intelligence are more capable of navigating interpersonal dynamics, maintaining composure, and fostering cooperation in emotionally demanding contexts such as classrooms. Moreover, the study suggests that emotional competence not only enhances pedagogical effectiveness but also protects teachers from stress and burnout, reinforcing its importance as a core component of professional excellence and success in education. 

The quantitative analysis of this study demonstrated a strong and statistically significant correlation between emotional intelligence levels and the quality of teacher-student interactions. Teachers who exhibited higher scores in emotional awareness, empathy, and self-regulation consistently reported fewer behavioral conflicts, improved communication, and stronger emotional bonds with their students. These findings confirm that emotional competence directly enhances the classroom atmosphere by promoting understanding, respect, and psychological safety in the classroom. Teachers who can manage their emotions effectively are better able to respond calmly to challenges and maintain constructive relationships with learners. This evidence aligns with Jennings and Greenberg's (2009) conclusions, who argued that emotionally intelligent teachers create prosocial learning environments that foster both academic achievement and socio-emotional development. Thus, the results of this study reinforce the view that emotional intelligence is a vital pedagogical asset that enables teachers to balance instructional demands with emotional connections and student-centered care. 

The qualitative interviews provided valuable insights into the everyday emotional realities experienced by primary school teachers, revealing the intensity of the emotional demands inherent in their profession. Participants frequently described challenges such as emotional exhaustion, student behavioral difficulties, time pressure, and administrative expectations, all of which contributed to elevated stress levels. Despite these challenges, many teachers demonstrated resilience by employing various emotional regulation strategies, including self-reflection, mindfulness, emotional distancing, and peer support, to maintain composure and professional effectiveness.
</snippet>

Title: Emotional Intelligence and Effective Classroom Processes of Elementary Teachers
Snippet: This study examined the relationship between emotional intelligence and effective classroom processes of elementary teachers. Specifically, it determined the level of emotional intelligence in terms of self-awareness, selfregulation, motivation, empathy, and social skills, as well as the level of effective classroom processes in terms of classroom management, classroom learning environment, instructional effectiveness, and student–teacher relationship. It also investigated the significant relationship between these variables. A quantitative correlational research design was employed, involving 180 elementary teachers. Data were collected using a validated survey questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rho correlation. The findings revealed that teachers demonstrated a very satisfactory level of emotional intelligence across all dimensions, with empathy and social skills obtaining the highest ratings. Similarly, teachers exhibited highly effective classroom processes, particularly in student–teacher relationships and classroom learning environment. Moreover, the results showed a statistically significant positive relationship between emotional intelligence and effective classroom processes (p < 0.05), indicating that higher levels of emotional intelligence are associated with more effective classroom practices. Among the components, social skills and empathy showed the strongest correlations. The study concludes that emotional intelligence significantly contributes to effective classroom processes. It is therefore recommended that schools implement professional development programs focusing on emotional intelligence, particularly in enhancing teachers’ interpersonal competencies to improve teaching effectiveness and student outcomes.

# Overview: Big Five personality in EFL/ESL teacher contexts

The Big Five model—openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism/emotional stability—has been applied to English as a Foreign/Second Language (EFL/ESL) teachers and trainees to understand how relatively stable individual differences relate to classroom behaviors, reflective practice, emotional regulation, and student outcomes.<cite id="0c139ee0-4">The Big Five framework has been widely adopted in organizational and applied research because it is valid, parsimonious, and supported by strong evidence, and it conceptualizes personality as relatively stable patterns of cognition, affect, and behavior</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-1">Big Five traits have been linked to reflective teaching among Iranian EFL teachers, motivating empirical work on trait–practice associations in EFL</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-4">Reviews of successful ESL/EFL teachers identify a set of characteristic strengths that map onto interpersonal, self-regulatory, and openness-related dispositions</cite>. Across studies, extraversion, conscientiousness, and neuroticism frequently emerge as strongest for day-to-day classroom processes and student interactions, whereas openness and agreeableness show more nuanced or indirect relationships to core EFL pedagogy, depending on context and outcome.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism are closely tied to EFL processes and outcomes; extraversion supports participation and oral development, conscientiousness supports organization and self-control for learning tasks, and neuroticism relates to anxiety that can hinder engagement</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-1">Openness and agreeableness are less directly tied to core EFL tasks that require sustained effort (e.g., vocabulary, reading), with weaker or inconsistent associations to EFL effectiveness</cite>.

# How Big Five has been measured in EFL/ESL

EFL/ESL studies commonly use validated Big Five instruments (e.g., BFI; NEO-based short forms) adapted for local populations, with robust internal consistency and convergent validity.<cite id="0c139ee0-0">The Big Five Inventory (BFI) has been adapted for EFL learners to assess the five domains (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness) using 44–46 items on a 5-point Likert scale</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-2">BFI domains (8–10 items) show acceptable internal consistency (e.g., α≈0.62–0.83 overall; openness α≈0.75), supporting its use for prospective teachers</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">A shortened Chinese NEO-based Big Five for university teachers (35 items) shows high internal consistency (α≈0.81–0.90) and structural validity, with all dimensions loading well</cite>. In teacher education settings, Big Five assessments have been paired with measures of pedagogical skills or reflective practice to model teacher development and selection-relevant profiles.<cite id="0c139ee0-3">Among 277 Malaysian TESL trainees, Big Five profiles were linked to verbal communication skills, a core pedagogical competence</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-1">Studies in Iranian EFL teacher cohorts explicitly test relationships between Big Five traits and reflective teaching quality</cite>.

# Trait-by-trait evidence in EFL/ESL contexts

Openness to experience. In EFL/ESL trainees, openness shows the clearest positive linkage to verbal/linguistic communication behaviors, suggesting value for fostering interactive language use and creativity in EFL classes.<cite id="0c139ee0-3">Only openness among Big Five traits positively related to verbal communication skills in Malaysian TESL trainees, warranting emphasis to maximize effective communication</cite>. In Chinese university teacher samples, openness is measured reliably and theoretically tied to receptivity to novel ideas and tasks; however, some EFL learner-focused work argues that openness contributes less directly to core EFL effectiveness than self-regulatory and sociable traits.<cite id="f67e7d50-0">Big Five dimensions (including openness) exhibit strong psychometric structure in Chinese university teachers</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-1">Openness is more strongly associated with creativity-oriented domains than with sustained effort tasks central to EFL learning</cite>.

Conscientiousness. Conscientious teachers tend to be more organized, disciplined, and goal-directed, which maps onto lesson planning, materials management, and independent learner support—key to EFL effectiveness.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness is characterized by goal orientation and self-discipline, aligning with systematic study practices (e.g., vocabulary memorization, grammar note-taking) that directly enhance language outcomes</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Prior EFL work indicates teachers’ affective/surgency and personality factors (including conscientious traits) impact students’ achievement and motivation</cite>. Among EFL/ESL instructors, conscientiousness is repeatedly implicated in student attainment and classroom organization, reinforcing its salience for EFL contexts.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Studies report extroversion and friendliness contribute to student success, and broader EFL evidence links teachers’ affective factors to attainment</cite>.

Extraversion. Extraversion (surgency/affectivity) is consistently linked to classroom rapport, participation, and management, which are critical in communicative EFL classes.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">EFL/ESL studies emphasize the effectiveness of teachers’ extroversion and friendliness for students’ success, especially with adult learners</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">A comparative study of extroverted vs. introverted EFL teachers in Iran found extroverted teachers reported more proficient class management and students perceived content more positively and showed greater motivation</cite>. Direct EFL teacher evidence also shows strong positive correlations between overall Big Five profiles and classroom management quality, with extraversion contributing to lively, inspirational environments.<cite id="4f2bf94b-0">A quantitative study of Palestinian EFL teachers found strong positive correlations between Big Five traits and effective classroom management practices</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Well-adjusted emotional and affective personality helps teachers develop lively and inspirational EFL learning environments</cite>.

Agreeableness. Agreeableness aligns with empathy, cooperation, and interpersonal harmony, supporting student–teacher rapport and collaborative learning; however, direct links to core EFL task performance are often weaker or indirect compared to conscientiousness and extraversion.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Agreeableness (empathy/cooperation) may be less directly tied to core EFL tasks that rely on individual effort, with weaker or inconsistent links to EFL effectiveness</cite>. Teacher-education studies that include reflective practice emphasize that agreeableness can shape how teachers engage peers and mediate conflicts, which indirectly supports EFL classroom climate.<cite id="0c139ee0-1">Big Five traits, including agreeableness, relate to reflective teaching, affecting how teachers interact and problem-solve in EFL contexts</cite>.

Neuroticism (low emotional stability). Higher neuroticism is associated with anxiety and self-doubt that can undermine engagement and persistence; in teacher contexts, it tends to correlate negatively with effective classroom processes, whereas lower neuroticism supports emotional regulation and calm instruction.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Neurotic learners (and by extension neurotic teachers) are prone to anxiety and self-doubt, which can hinder engagement and persistence in EFL tasks</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Teachers’ positive personality traits and wellbeing correlate with effective practices; in contrast, no association with stressors highlights the role of adaptive regulation</cite>. Emotional self-regulation research shows that teachers with stronger regulation report fewer behavioral conflicts and stronger student–teacher bonds, consistent with lower trait neuroticism supporting classroom processes.<cite id="7065a9a1-2">Teachers with stronger self-regulation and empathy reported fewer behavioral conflicts, improved communication, and stronger emotional bonds with students</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-3">Emotional intelligence was positively associated with classroom management, learning environment, instruction, and relationships; social skills and empathy showed the strongest correlations</cite>.

Mechanisms: emotional regulation and affective climate
Multiple EFL studies indicate that personality-linked affectivity and surgency interact with emotional regulation to shape classroom dynamics and student outcomes.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Personality-linked extroversion and friendliness contribute to students’ success; extraversion fosters lively, inspirational environments</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extraversion/introversion differences yielded significant differences in class management and student motivation in EFL settings</cite>. In Chinese university EFL contexts, Big Five measures have been used to model how openness, conscientiousness, and agreeableness interplay with emotion regulation to affect classroom engagement, suggesting that self-regulation mediates trait–outcome links.<cite id="f67e7d50-0">A Big Five–based model of Chinese university teachers linked teacher personality to students’ classroom engagement with a mediating role of emotional regulation</cite>. Broad teacher research shows that emotional intelligence—self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, social skills—correlates with and improves classroom processes (management, relationships, learning environment), providing a plausible pathway from Big Five (especially conscientiousness and extraversion; lower neuroticism) to effective EFL practice.<cite id="7065a9a1-3">Emotional intelligence was positively associated with effective classroom processes (management, relationships, learning environment, instruction)</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-2">Higher emotional intelligence supported fewer conflicts and stronger bonds, consistent with emotionally intelligent teachers creating prosocial learning environments</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-0">Emotional intelligence significantly predicted teachers’ conflict management (β≈0.49, R²≈0.24), supporting mediation pathways from affective traits to classroom effectiveness</cite>.

# Cross-cultural patterns and contextual moderators

Across cultures, the Big Five–to–teaching effectiveness link is robust, but the relative salience of traits can shift with educational norms and classroom demands. In Palestinian EFL schools, overall Big Five strongly correlates with classroom management, highlighting generalizability of the pattern.<cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Big Five traits showed a strong positive correlation with effective classroom management among Palestinian EFL teachers</cite>. In Iran, EFL teacher studies tie Big Five to reflective practice and show extroverted teachers manage classes more proficiently and motivate students better, aligning with extraversion’s role in interactive pedagogy.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extroverted EFL teachers reported more proficient class management; students in extroverted teachers’ classes perceived content better and were more motivated</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-1">Big Five traits relate to reflective teaching among Iranian EFL teachers</cite>. In Malaysia, only openness among trainee teachers correlated positively with verbal communication, pointing to culture- and curriculum-specific emphases (e.g., communicative competence in EFL).<cite id="0c139ee0-3">Only openness positively related to verbal communication among Malaysian TESL trainees, recommending greater attention to communication skills</cite>. In China, both psychometric validity and conceptual analyses indicate conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism are most consequential for EFL processes and outcomes, with openness and agreeableness less directly tied to core tasks; conversely, Big Five profiles have been modeled as affecting classroom engagement through emotional regulation.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism are closely related to EFL processes and effectiveness; openness and agreeableness show weaker or inconsistent associations</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">Chinese university teachers’ Big Five shows strong structural validity and links to student engagement via emotional regulation</cite>. These patterns align with cross-disciplinary findings that extraversion and conscientiousness generally predict teacher effectiveness and student engagement, while emotional stability moderates stress and burnout risks in demanding educational settings.<cite id="7065a9a1-2">Emotion regulation strategies help teachers maintain composure and effectiveness amid high emotional demands</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-4">Emotional intelligence accounts for substantial variance in discipline strategies and supports behavior management and overall success</cite>.

# Practical implications for EFL teacher selection, development, and research

- Selection and profiling: Prioritize conscientiousness, extraversion, openness to experience, and lower neuroticism as initial markers for EFL teacher candidates, with attention to openness when programs emphasize creativity and content-creation. Validate locally using adapted BFI/NEO instruments with demonstrated reliability and cultural fit.<cite id="0c139ee0-0">BFI provides established psychometric coverage for EFL populations</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">NEO-based Chinese Big Five shows strong reliability and validity for university teachers</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Big Five correlates positively with classroom management in EFL teaching settings</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-3">Openness uniquely predicted verbal communication skills among TESL trainees</cite>.
- Developmental levers: Target emotional intelligence and self-regulation training to amplify the effects of core traits—improving classroom climate, behavior management, and rapport—especially for introverted or neurotic teachers seeking to build energizing, organized classes.<cite id="7065a9a1-3">Emotional intelligence training improved teachers’ interpersonal competencies and classroom processes</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-0">Emotional intelligence significantly predicted conflict management among teachers</cite>.
- Cultural tailoring: In cultures emphasizing rote learning and compliance, strengthen conscientiousness and emotional stability; in communicative, interaction-focused EFL programs, emphasize extraversion, openness, and reflective practice to foster participation and motivation.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness and extraversion map onto concrete EFL task effectiveness</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extroversion and friendliness boost student success, with extroverted EFL teachers managing classes more effectively</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-3">Openness uniquely linked to verbal communication in Malaysian trainees</cite>.
- Measurement and fairness: Use locally validated instruments and triangulate personality with classroom observations and student outcomes to avoid overreliance on self-report and to align traits with EFL-specific competencies (e.g., speaking interaction, writing feedback, materials organization).<cite id="f67e7d50-0">Local adaptation of Big Five maintains psychometric integrity and supports culture-specific modeling</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Quantitative links between Big Five and classroom management provide outcome-relevant validation</cite>.

# Limitations and open questions

Evidence is strongest for associations—correlations and quasi-experimental contrasts—rather than causal effects; mediation via emotion regulation is plausible but needs more EFL-specific longitudinal studies. Trait salience may vary by school type (public vs. private), learner age, and proficiency level; more cross-cultural meta-analyses focused on EFL teacher cohorts would clarify effect sizes and moderators. Finally, agreeableness and openness may matter more for collegial and curriculum contexts (e.g., team teaching, project-based EFL) where individual task persistence is less central, but direct EFL outcome evidence remains mixed.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Openness and agreeableness may be less directly tied to core EFL task effectiveness, though they can influence creativity-oriented domains</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-4">Despite widespread use of Big Five, there remains a paucity of studies directly linking Big Five traits to reflective teaching in EFL, calling for more applied research</cite>.

# Bottom line: Big Five traits that tend to characterize effective EFL teachers

- Extraversion: energizes interaction, rapport, and classroom management; linked to higher student motivation and positive perception in EFL settings.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extroverted teachers reported more proficient class management; students in extroverted teachers’ classes were more motivated and had better perception</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Big Five strongly correlates with effective classroom management in Palestinian EFL teachers</cite>.
- Conscientiousness: supports organization, planning, and disciplined instruction; directly tied to language-learning routines and student attainment patterns in EFL.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Conscientiousness promotes goal-directed, self-disciplined study behaviors that enhance language outcomes</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Teachers’ affective/surgency and personality factors contribute to student success</cite>.
- Openness to experience: fosters creativity, receptivity to novel content, and communicative fluency; especially relevant for interactive and creative EFL tasks and teacher–trainee communication.<cite id="0c139ee0-3">Openness uniquely predicted verbal communication skills among EFL/ESL trainees</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">Openness shows strong structural validity in Chinese university teachers</cite>.
- Agreeableness: aids empathy, collaboration, and conflict resolution, indirectly supporting EFL climate and participation; direct links to core task performance are weaker or inconsistent.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Agreeableness is less directly tied to core EFL tasks; shows weaker or inconsistent associations with EFL effectiveness</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-1">Big Five relates to reflective teaching, which often involves empathic, collaborative stances</cite>.
- Emotional stability (low neuroticism): reduces anxiety and emotional volatility, enabling calm, consistent instruction and better behavior management; higher neuroticism is associated with challenges in persistence and classroom composure.<cite id="f67e7d50-1">Neurotic learners are prone to anxiety and self-doubt, hindering EFL engagement; by extension, higher neuroticism can undermine teacher effectiveness</cite><cite id="7065a9a1-2">Self-regulation and empathy reduce conflicts and build stronger student–teacher bonds</cite>.

Taken together, effective EFL teachers typically exhibit high extraversion and conscientiousness, openness to experience aligned with program goals, agreeableness for collaborative climate, and low neuroticism supported by strong emotional regulation, with implementation details shifting across cultures and curricula.<cite id="4f2bf94b-1">Extraversion and conscientiousness are repeatedly linked to EFL classroom effectiveness and student outcomes</cite><cite id="f67e7d50-0">Chinese university teacher Big Five modeling shows openness, conscientiousness, and agreeableness structure and links to engagement via regulation</cite><cite id="0c139ee0-3">Openness uniquely supports verbal communication in EFL/ESL trainee samples</cite><cite id="4f2bf94b-0">Overall Big Five correlates strongly with classroom management among EFL teachers</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Influence of Personality and Learning Styles in English Language Achievement
Snippet: In this study, the Big Five Inventory (BFI) was administered to determine the personality traits of EFL learners for a robust measure of personality traits established by previous researchers John and Srivastava [36]. The BFI was adopted from John et al. [37] consists of forty six items intended to evaluate the big five personality traits, whereas eight statements were for the domain Extraversion and neuroticism, nine for the domain agreeableness and conscientiousness and ten for openness domains. These statements are for self-report and scored according to a five point Likert-type (strongly agree, agree, neutral, disagree and strongly disagree).

Title: On the Relationship between Reflective Teaching and Personality Traits
Snippet: What are the characteristics of teacher reflectivity regarding big five personality traits? RQ2: Are there any relationships between Big Five Personality traits and reflective teaching among Iranian EFL teachers?

Title: Impact of Big five personality traits on Academic Achievement of Prospective Teachers
Snippet: Researcher used the questionnaire as a research instrument to conduct this study. The instrument was consisted of two sections. 1. Demographic profile which consisted of gender, University name and cumulative grade point (CGPA). Prospective teachers were asked to report their CGPA from their previous semester. 2. Big Five personality traits, which was measured by using Big five inventory (BFI) (John, 1991). Big five inventory (BFI) (John, 1991) was adapted to collect the responses for Big five traits from the prospective teachers. This inventory was further divided into 5 domains including 8 to 10 items per domain. First domain was named extraversion, which consisted of 8 statements. Second domain was named agreeableness which consisted of 9 statements. Third domain was named Conscientiousness which consisted of 9 statements. Fourth domain was named neuroticism which consisted of 8 statements. Fifth domain was named openness to experience which consisted of 10 statements. Total 44 statements were included in this inventory. Each statement in BFI was presented on a 5 point type Likert scale According to the John (1991), the developer of the inventory; the BFI has an internal consistency of.83. The following Cronbach coefficient alphas were calculated in the present study: extraversion, 0.62; Agreeableness, 0.67; Conscientiousness, 0.69; Neuroticism, 0.72; Openness to experience, 0.75. Overall the reliability of the instrument was 0.79.

Title: TESL Trainee Practitioners’ Self Perception of their Personality Traits and Verbal Communication Skills
Snippet: The teaching and learning of English as a second language involve many different skills. This study investigates the relationship between Teaching English as a Second Language (TESL) trainee practitioners’ (TPs) personality traits and their verbal communication skills. The personality traits investigated are the Big Five, while the verbal communication skills investigated include interpersonal skills, verbal-linguistic skills, motivation, altruism, and self-regulation. This study involved 277 TESL TPs from four different teacher training institutes in Malaysia. This quantitative study used  questionnaires to investigate both the variables. The findings show that out of the Big Five personality traits, only openness showed positive relationship to verbal communication. This trait deserves greater attention if students are to maximise the use of effective communication skills. This study profiles personality traits to examine the relationship of each trait in relation to communication skills. The findings of this study would be significant for the Higher Education Ministry of Malaysia and education regulators, apart from the teaching community.

Title: On the Relationship between Reflective Teaching and Personality Traits
Snippet: There is an apparent paucity of studies concerning the association between the Big Five personality traits and reflective teaching. Personality traits have a big influence on how teachers reflect on their teaching methods and strategies. This indicates that the personalities of teachers are important to their teaching perspectives and may even determine them. Thus, it is postulated here that each instructor with a unique personality trait favors specific components of teaching reflections. The Big Five Inventory was made up in the late 1980s as a very short instrument to measure personality. Tit was a short instrument at that time as it contained 44 short-phrase items which would be responded within the span of 5 minutes and were enough to assess the Big Five Dimension. (Rammstedt & John, 2007). The Big Five or the model of personality based on five personality explains the personalities completely and solid evidence is also available to support this. (Bose & Sgori,2022;Elaskary 2021) The big five has been used up in recent organizations and many applied research because it is widely accepted, and it is a valid technique of measuring personality traits. (Chiorri et al., 2015) LITERATURE REVIEW Personality traits include relatively stable patterns of cognitions, beliefs, and behaviors. The Big Five model has functioned as the powerful theoretical framework to synthesize most of the variation in these patterns (McCrae & Costa, 2008). The roots of this model lie in two research traditions: the psycho-lexical approach and the questionnaire approach (De Raad & Perugini, 2002;John & Srivastava, 1999). The Big Five model was discovered and originally verified within psycho-lexical studies founded on the lexical hypothesis, which states that all personality traits are encoded in every natural language (Cattell, 1943;Goldberg, 1981Goldberg, , 1990)). The words invented and used to describe individual differences are exactly the same with how the trait terms have been used in the lexical approach. Identification of personality traits in the lexical approach is guided by two criteria: synonym frequency (i.e., the more important is a personality attribute, the more synonyms are used to describe it within the language) and cross-cultural universality (i.e., the most phenotypic attributes are typically codified in terms in the languages of different cultures).

Title: Effectiveness of Big Five Traits on Classroom Management in Teaching English Language in Palestinian Schools
Snippet: Teachers have a critical influence on the success or failure of any educational institution. The effectiveness of teachers is thought to be the most important component in influencing pupils’ academic progress. This paper is intended to find out the effectiveness of Big Five Traits toward classroom management in English language teaching in Palestinian schools. This study used a fully quantitative method with a survey as its data collection method where the participants were 35 elementary school teachers. Out of the total number of the participants, 45.7% were females, 34.3% were aged between 23-30 or 31-40 years old, 85.7% had Bachelor’s degrees, and 37.1% reported having over 10 years of teaching experience. The result of this study showed that there was a strong positive correlation between the teachers’ big five personality traits and their effective classroom management practices.

Title: A Review of the Impact of EFL Teachers’ Affectivity and Surgency and Learners’ Shyness on Their Language Attainment
Snippet: Teachers' characteristics, including personality and affective factors, have proved influential on learners' motivation and achievement, particularly in EFL/ESL classes. Moreover, it is crucial for teachers to promote social interactions with students to develop their learning capacity. For instance, Eryilmaz (2014) argued that a well-adjusted emotional and affective personality can help teachers develop a lively and inspirational learning environment. Meanwhile, the study confirms the effectiveness of teachers' extroversion and friendliness in students' success, especially adult learners. MacIntyre et al. (2019) aimed to assess the correlation between language teachers' personality and well-being and stressful situations and stressors. Forty-seven EFL/ESL university instructors participated in this study. They employed the big five personality scale (including extroversion), the PERMA wellbeing framework, and a stressor scale to measure these variables. The results of the study indicated a positive relationship between teachers' personality traits and their well-being; nonetheless, no association was found between personality traits and stressors. Furthermore, Garcia et al. (2011) employed the big five inventory to examine the correlation between teachers' personality type and secondary students' attainment. They concluded that teachers' affective factors can have a substantial impact on learners' achievement. 

Jalili and Mall-Amiri (2015) used Eysenck Personality Inventory to evaluate female teachers' extroversion/introversion characteristics. Then, they selected thirty extroverted and thirty introverted instructors teaching English in private institutes in Tehran, Iran. This study aimed to assess EFL teachers' class Tian EFL Teachers' Affectivity management based on their personality type. The findings demonstrated a significant difference between the two groups of teachers, where extroverted teachers reported performing more proficiently in managing EFL classes. Similarly, Dost et al. (2017) confirmed that extroverted teachers were more successful in class management; besides, they concluded that students in the extroverted teacher group showed an outstanding perception of the course content and were highly motivated to learn English compared to the students in the introverted teacher classroom. 

It is also noteworthy that Binti (2014) asserted that psychologists believe attitudes, inspiration, perceptions, and capabilities form individuals' personalities.

Title: The Impact of Teachers’ Personality on Senior High School EFL Learners’ General English Achievement
Snippet: This study is primarily designed to discover the effect of teachers' personality on the EFL learners' general English achievement at the pre-intermediate level. A study of this kind can possibly uncover valuable information to aid teachers in improving their personality to enhance the students' general English achievement. The objective of this study is to examine the impact of teachers' personality on senior high school EFL learners' general English achievement. Moreover, the objective of this study was also to examine how the teachers' personality can influence their teaching effectiveness. 

The study may be significant if it directly deals with helping teachers to recognize the importance of their personality role in enhancing students' achievement and general English achievement. Although there are other factors (e.g., sex, attitude, motivation, etc.) which contribute to the achievement of the students, English teachers need to be cognizant of the fact that their personality will have positive and negative effects on the achievements of their students. This study may be significant since it would help teachers to think of their personality, achieve more skills, or succeed in teaching English as a foreign language (EFL). It could reveal some of information on the teachers' personality and teaching method and their effects on students who learn EFL.IT may be helpful for formulating different teaching strategies to overcome the students' problems. This research may pave the way for future research studies in the same field. Furthermore, findings of this study would greatly benefit the Ministry of Education in primary and secondary schools. 

The teachers may know themselves to integrate their personality strength to make their teaching techniques more effective needed in achieving the educational development as well as achieving their own pedagogical goals. REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE Personality comes from the Latin word'' charm'', which means mask, face shield or even a sound (personae). The purpose of this refers to the outward appearance of an individual. According to psychologists (e.g., Binti, 2014) personality includes thoughts, perceptions, values, attitudes, character, ability, confidence, intelligence, motivation, habits and so on. Mischel (1999) stated the concept of personality as the dynamic organization psychophysical systems that determine individual's behavior and thinking. In everyday life, we cannot deny the fact that we are too hard to realize ourselves to be fully human perfection. We can only make ourselves as fully functional human beings.

Title: On the Relationship between Reflective Teaching and Personality Traits
Snippet: He is regarded as a forefather of current personality study. Traits are viewed as elements of emotional, motivational, and social behavior. They are hypothesized to define and explain individual variations in human behavior and experience, as well as to forecast them (Cohn et al., 2020;Fröhlich et al., 2022;McCrae & Costa, 2008). professional needs and development (Naemah, 2007). 

Reflection is core to sustaining effective professional development in teacher education and teaching practices (Dewey, 1909;Feucht, 2010;Pall, 2022;Schoen, 1987). Teachers will often reflect on their teaching practices, evidenced by the ways they communicate with peers about current and critical issues, mindful introspection, and systematic research methodologies. Reflective teaching is an active educational activity. Reflective teaching practice in second/foreign language teaching education has grown in popularity over the last thirty years, attracting the attention of academics since the early 1990s (Richards, 1991). However, despite this progress, there is still a lack of study on the attitudes of reflective instructors as indicated in their reflections in the English language teaching setting (Farrell, 2012). Meanwhile, it is believed that acknowledging the advantages of being a reflective teacher might assist us in committing to our own professional development (Alsuhaibani, 2020). (Gordon et al., 2006), define teacher effectiveness as a measure of job performance in the teaching profession that can reflect the impact a teacher has had while completing their duties. Thus, we can hypothesis about the potential relationships each of the Big Five domains (conscientiousness, emotional stability, extraversion, agreeableness, and openness) may have with teacher effectiveness using both organizational and educational psychology studies.

Title: An associative model of Chinese university teachers' personality traits and students' classroom engagement from the teacher's perspective: the mediating role of emotional regulation
Snippet: Teacher personality was assessed using a shortened Chinese version of the Big Five Inventory, based on the NEO framework (Xu, 2019). The scale comprises 35 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale, measuring five first-order dimensions: extraversion (seven items), agreeableness (seven items), conscientiousness (seven items), neuroticism (seven items), and openness to experience (seven items). In the current sample, the sub-scales demonstrated high internal consistency, with Cronbach's α ranging from 0.812 to 0.903, and an overall scale α of 0.893. Standardized factor loadings for all dimensions exceeded 0.47, with Openness, Conscientiousness, and Agreeableness surpassing 0.90, confirming the structural integrity and convergent validity of the Big Five construct.

Title: The mediating role of emotion regulation in the link between personality traits and self-regulated learning among low-achieving EFL learners
Snippet: To explore personality traits, this study adopts the Five-Factor Model of Personality (FFM), given its wide validation in conceptualizing personality in the field of education 18 . The full spectrum of the FFM comprises five traits: conscientiousness (featured by goal orientation and self-discipline), openness to experience (featured by curiosity and imagination), extraversion (featured by sociability), agreeableness (featured by empathy and cooperation), and neuroticism (featured by emotional instability). Specifically, this study focuses on conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism but excludes openness and agreeableness for three reasons. First, conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism are closely related to the EFL learning process and its effectiveness. For instance, conscientious learners, with strong organisation and self-control, often engage in systematic practices like vocabulary memorisation and grammar note-taking, which can directly enhance language outcomes 5 . Extraverted students, who are usually more outgoing and social, are more inclined to participate in speaking activities and thus support oral English development 5 . In contrast, neurotic learners, prone to anxiety and self-doubt, may struggle with engagement and persistence in the demanding process of EFL learning 19 . Second, prior research has identified these three traits as significant predictors of EFL performance 5,20 . Third, openness to experience and agreeableness are less relevant to core EFL learning tasks. Specifically, openness to experience, which emphasises imagination and novelty, is more strongly associated with creativity-oriented domains such as art or literature 21 , rather than with the sustained effort and persistence required in EFL learning. Similarly, agreeableness, which reflects interpersonal harmony, appears to be less directly relevant to core EFL tasks that rely heavily on individual efforts (e.g., vocabulary acquisition and reading comprehension). Also, empirical studies have also suggested that openness and agreeableness demonstrate weaker or inconsistent associations with EFL effectiveness 5 . Given these considerations, the present study focuses on exploring conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism as the key personality traits influencing the EFL learning process.

Title: Cyber-Personality and Liking Expression: A Study From WeChat Users in China
Snippet: In the main study, we measured the Big-Five personality traits using the 60 items of the NEO-FFI inventory (Costa and McCrae, 1992). The inventory assesses five personality traits: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, emotional stability, and openness to experience. The Chinese version of this inventory had been used and tested previously (Yao and Liang, 2010). Participants responded to the items on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). The Cronbach's alpha coefficients in the present study were 0.86 for extroversion, 0.83 for conscientiousness, 0.70 for agreeableness, 0.66 for openness, and 0.81 for neuroticism (emotional stability).

Title: How blindness shapes personality: a neuro-ecological account
Snippet: All participants completed the Chinese version of the NEO-Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI) (Costa and McCrae, 1992), a 60-item Big Five personality traits questionnaire. This inventory has been repeatedly used in different Chinese populations and has been shown to have satisfactory validity and reliability (Yang et al., 1999;Zhang, 2003;Yu and Zhang, 2007). The Big Five personality traits include five dimensions: neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. Neuroticism is related to emotional stability and self-regulatory abilities. Extraversion refers to the degree of extroversion and sociability. Openness reflects the willingness to accept new ideas, experiences, and possibilities. Agreeableness refers to friendly attitudes and behaviors towards others and society. Conscientiousness reflects one's organization, reliability, and selfdiscipline. Each item was rated on a five-point Likert scale from 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree). After reverse scoring where appropriate, higher scores indicated stronger representation of the respective trait.

In the current sample, the sub-scales demonstrated high internal consistency, with Cronbach's α ranging from 0.812 to 0.903, and an overall scale α of 0.893. Standardized factor loadings for all dimensions exceeded 0.47, with Openness, Conscientiousness, and Agreeableness surpassing 0.90, confirming the structural integrity and convergent validity of the Big Five construct.

documents.title: The mediating role of emotion regulation in the link between personality traits and self-regulated learning among low-achieving EFL learners
documents.snippet: To explore personality traits, this study adopts the Five-Factor Model of Personality (FFM), given its wide validation in conceptualizing personality in the field of education 18 . The full spectrum of the FFM comprises five traits: conscientiousness (featured by goal orientation and self-discipline), openness to experience (featured by curiosity and imagination), extraversion (featured by sociability), agreeableness (featured by empathy and cooperation), and neuroticism (featured by emotional instability). Specifically, this study focuses on conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism but excludes openness and agreeableness for three reasons. First, conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism are closely related to the EFL learning process and its effectiveness. For instance, conscientious learners, with strong organisation and self-control, often engage in systematic practices like vocabulary memorisation and grammar note-taking, which can directly enhance language outcomes 5 . Extraverted students, who are usually more outgoing and social, are more inclined to participate in speaking activities and thus support oral English development 5 . In contrast, neurotic learners, prone to anxiety and self-doubt, may struggle with engagement and persistence in the demanding process of EFL learning 19 . Second, prior research has identified these three traits as significant predictors of EFL performance 5,20 . Third, openness to experience and agreeableness are less relevant to core EFL learning tasks. Specifically, openness to experience, which emphasises imagination and novelty, is more strongly associated with creativity-oriented domains such as art or literature 21 , rather than with the sustained effort and persistence required in EFL learning. Similarly, agreeableness, which reflects interpersonal harmony, appears to be less directly relevant to core EFL tasks that rely heavily on individual efforts (e.g., vocabulary acquisition and reading comprehension). Also, empirical studies have also suggested that openness and agreeableness demonstrate weaker or inconsistent associations with EFL effectiveness 5 . Given these considerations, the present study focuses on exploring conscientiousness, extraversion, and neuroticism as the key personality traits influencing the EFL learning process.

documents.snippet: In the main study, we measured the Big-Five personality traits using the 60 items of the NEO-FFI inventory (Costa and McCrae, 1992). The inventory assesses five personality traits: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, emotional stability, and openness to experience. The Chinese version of this inventory had been used and tested previously (Yao and Liang, 2010). Participants responded to the items on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). The Cronbach's alpha coefficients in the present study were 0.86 for extroversion, 0.83 for conscientiousness, 0.70 for agreeableness, 0.66 for openness, and 0.81 for neuroticism (emotional stability).

documents.title: How blindness shapes personality: a neuro-ecological account
documents.snippet: All participants completed the Chinese version of the NEO-Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI) (Costa and McCrae, 1992), a 60-item Big Five personality traits questionnaire. This inventory has been repeatedly used in different Chinese populations and has been shown to have satisfactory validity and reliability (Yang et al., 1999;Zhang, 2003;Yu and Zhang, 2007). The Big Five personality traits include five dimensions: neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. Neuroticism is related to emotional stability and self-regulatory abilities. Extraversion refers to the degree of extroversion and sociability. Openness reflects the willingness to accept new ideas, experiences, and possibilities. Agreeableness refers to friendly attitudes and behaviors towards others and society. Conscientiousness reflects one's organization, reliability, and selfdiscipline. Each item was rated on a five-point Likert scale from 0 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree). After reverse scoring where appropriate, higher scores indicated stronger representation of the respective trait.

Title: Effects of Emotional Intelligence on Conflict Management (Survey of Secondary School Teachers in Dera Ismail Khan, Pakistan)
Snippet: Emotional intelligence (EI) has emerged as a critical determinant of effective interpersonal behavior within educational institutions. Teachers who understand, regulate, and utilize emotions constructively can transform classroom conflicts into opportunities for collaboration and growth. This study aimed to assess the relationship between emotional intelligence and conflict-management abilities among secondary-school teachers in Dera Ismail Khan, Pakistan, while examining gender- and experience-based variations. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was adopted. Data were collected from 300 teachers using the Emotional Intelligence Scale for Teachers (Dey & Ratan, 2022) and Rahim’s Organizational Conflict Inventory–II Form B (Rahim, 2002). Reliability values were satisfactory (α = 0.831 for EI; α = 0.885 for conflict management). Pearson’s correlation (r = 0.492, p < 0.001) showed a significant positive association between EI and conflict management. Regression analysis confirmed that EI significantly predicted conflict management (β = 0.492, R² = 0.242). Female teachers scored higher on emotional intelligence, while male teachers exhibited stronger conflict-management skills (p < 0.001). ANOVA revealed significant differences across age, qualification, and service length (p ≤ 0.05). The findings suggest that emotionally competent teachers are better equipped to resolve interpersonal disputes and create positive learning environments. These results align with organizational behavior research showing that emotional regulation reduces resource depletion and enhances productivity (Javeed & Siddique, 2024). Integrating EI training into teacher development programs is recommended to enhance conflict resolution skills and overall institutional harmony. These results reinforce the role of emotional regulation in organizational behavior and align with recent findings linking psychological resources and workplace effectiveness (Javeed & Siddique, 2025).
