Title: Psychological features of emotional relationships in primary school teachers
Snippet: The results of this study reveal the complex and multifaceted nature of emotional relationships within primary school teachers' professional experiences. The findings underscore that emotional intelligence, especially components such as self-regulation, empathy, and emotional awareness, plays a crucial role in determining the quality and stability of teacher-student relationships. Teachers who demonstrate strong emotional control and empathy can create supportive, trusting, and productive learning environments. These results are consistent with the theoretical perspectives of Goleman (2005) and Salovey and Sluyter (1997), who emphasized that individuals with high emotional intelligence are more capable of navigating interpersonal dynamics, maintaining composure, and fostering cooperation in emotionally demanding contexts such as classrooms. Moreover, the study suggests that emotional competence not only enhances pedagogical effectiveness but also protects teachers from stress and burnout, reinforcing its importance as a core component of professional excellence and success in education. 

The quantitative analysis of this study demonstrated a strong and statistically significant correlation between emotional intelligence levels and the quality of teacher-student interactions. Teachers who exhibited higher scores in emotional awareness, empathy, and self-regulation consistently reported fewer behavioral conflicts, improved communication, and stronger emotional bonds with their students. These findings confirm that emotional competence directly enhances the classroom atmosphere by promoting understanding, respect, and psychological safety in the classroom. Teachers who can manage their emotions effectively are better able to respond calmly to challenges and maintain constructive relationships with learners. This evidence aligns with Jennings and Greenberg's (2009) conclusions, who argued that emotionally intelligent teachers create prosocial learning environments that foster both academic achievement and socio-emotional development. Thus, the results of this study reinforce the view that emotional intelligence is a vital pedagogical asset that enables teachers to balance instructional demands with emotional connections and student-centered care. 

The qualitative interviews provided valuable insights into the everyday emotional realities experienced by primary school teachers, revealing the intensity of the emotional demands inherent in their profession. Participants frequently described challenges such as emotional exhaustion, student behavioral difficulties, time pressure, and administrative expectations, all of which contributed to elevated stress levels. Despite these challenges, many teachers demonstrated resilience by employing various emotional regulation strategies, including self-reflection, mindfulness, emotional distancing, and peer support, to maintain composure and professional effectiveness.

Title: Emotional Intelligence and Effective Classroom Processes of Elementary Teachers
Snippet: This study examined the relationship between emotional intelligence and effective classroom processes of elementary teachers. Specifically, it determined the level of emotional intelligence in terms of self-awareness, selfregulation, motivation, empathy, and social skills, as well as the level of effective classroom processes in terms of classroom management, classroom learning environment, instructional effectiveness, and student–teacher relationship. It also investigated the significant relationship between these variables. A quantitative correlational research design was employed, involving 180 elementary teachers. Data were collected using a validated survey questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rho correlation. The findings revealed that teachers demonstrated a very satisfactory level of emotional intelligence across all dimensions, with empathy and social skills obtaining the highest ratings. Similarly, teachers exhibited highly effective classroom processes, particularly in student–teacher relationships and classroom learning environment. Moreover, the results showed a statistically significant positive relationship between emotional intelligence and effective classroom processes (p < 0.05), indicating that higher levels of emotional intelligence are associated with more effective classroom practices. Among the components, social skills and empathy showed the strongest correlations. The study concludes that emotional intelligence significantly contributes to effective classroom processes. It is therefore recommended that schools implement professional development programs focusing on emotional intelligence, particularly in enhancing teachers’ interpersonal competencies to improve teaching effectiveness and student outcomes.

Title: The Impact of Emotional Intelligence on Teachers Self Efficacy and Academic Achievement
Snippet: Teachers' emotional intelligence, which refers to the ability to understand and manage both their own emotions and those of others, is a crucial factor that significantly impacts their effectiveness in managing classroom environments (Bar-On, 2014). A study conducted by Jeloudar et al. (2011) emphasizes a strong statistical correlation (p < 0.05) between teachers' emotional intelligence and the discipline strategies they employ. This significant finding highlights the essential role that emotional intelligence plays in shaping educators' approaches to classroom discipline, with research indicating that it accounts for an impressive 95% of the influence on their methods. Furthermore, Jeloudar et al. ( 2011) study revealed that emotional intelligence enhances teachers' abilities to manage behavior and contributes to their overall success in the educational setting. The considerable impact of emotional intelligence on classroom management dynamics underscores the importance of prioritizing this critical aspect in teacher training (Dolev & Leshem, 2016;Pozo-Rico & Sandoval, 2020). 

Notably, Tuluhan and Yalcinkaya (2018)assert that emotional intelligence skills are not solely innate; they can be developed through dedicated effort, ultimately leading to great achievements in the classroom. They advocate for the creation of targeted teacher training programs aimed at enhancing these vital emotional intelligence skills. These skills can be intentionally improved through "deliberate learning practices and self-reflection on classroom interactions" (Jeloudar et al., 2011, p. 101). Understanding the complex role of emotions in behavior management is essential for teachers, particularly those who may not fully recognize its significance (Alam, & Ahmad, 2018). Moreover, the Research highlights that emotional intelligence encompasses a range of skills, including empathy, selfawareness, and self-regulation (Jeloudar et al., 2011, Mattern & Bauer, 2014). 

Additionally, Garner et al. (2013) explored the relationship between emotion regulation styles, dispositional empathy, and perceptions of appropriate emotional responses among aspiring educators. Their research aimed to determine whether these factors could predict future teachers' attitudes toward bullying and their responses to instances of peer conflict.

Summary answer
Across EFL contexts, Big Five personality traits are positively associated with measures of teaching effectiveness and classroom management, supporting both selection and performance perspectives. Evidence indicates that pre-service candidates already show marked trait profiles (e.g., high conscientiousness), consistent with selection by fit, and that teacher socialization and professional development can shape how personality manifests in classrooms, suggesting some effectiveness-related change. However, Big Five is relatively stable across time and contexts, implying that self-selection into teaching and into EFL specifically plays a meaningful role, while professional development can still leverage trait-related growth to improve effectiveness. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">In a quantitative survey of EFL teachers in Palestinian schools, Big Five traits showed strong positive correlations with effective classroom management practices</cite> <cite id="a0b397f9-1">and an EFL study framed teachers’ personality as a lever that influences learners’ general English achievement and teaching effectiveness</cite> <cite id="a0b397f9-2">with Big Five predicting effectiveness among in-service primary English teachers</cite> <cite id="fe72db8f-1">and with reviews arguing that personal suitability data should complement academic criteria in teacher selection to recruit and retain more effective applicants</cite> <cite id="b53b20ea-2">and empirical work showing pre-service teachers already exhibit dominant Big Five profiles (e.g., high conscientiousness) before fieldwork</cite> <cite id="5d321988-0">while longitudinal student-focused work finds Big Five trait consistency in the face of teacher changes</cite> <cite id="5d321988-1">and EFL competency frameworks elevating personality as a core component</cite>.

What Big Five measures show in EFL classrooms
Empirical EFL studies consistently report that extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness correlate with teacher effectiveness, while neuroticism tends to relate negatively, albeit with context-specific moderators. <cite id="a0b397f9-2">In primary English teachers, extraversion and agreeableness (and to a lesser extent conscientiousness and openness) significantly predicted teacher effectiveness, with little impact from experience and qualifications, prompting suggestions to use personality in selection or development</cite>. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">In Palestinian EFL classrooms, all Big Five traits correlated positively with effective classroom management, a proximal mechanism for student achievement</cite>. <cite id="a0b397f9-1">An EFL study explicitly posited that teachers’ personality shapes learners’ general English achievement and called for recognizing and developing personality strengths to improve EFL outcomes</cite>. <cite id="5d321988-2">A recent EFL-focused sociopsychological study categorized “personality factors” as a core component of EFL teachers’ professional competencies, aligning with competency models that view stable personality alongside interpersonal, instructional, and contextual factors</cite>.

Does EFL teaching effectiveness reflect self-selection or trait-driven performance?
There are converging indications of both selection and performance effects. First, Big Five traits reliably predict valued work and educational outcomes, and teacher selection debates explicitly recommend incorporating “personal suitability” (personality) with academic scores to admit more effective candidates. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Reviews note that entry to teacher education is often based on academic criteria alone and argue that personal suitability should accompany academic criteria to recruit and retain more effective applicants; they call for identifying pre-teaching Big Five characteristics that predict teacher performance and student outcomes</cite>. <cite id="b53b20ea-2">Empirically, pre-service teachers already show dominant Big Five profiles—most commonly conscientiousness—before their practicum, consistent with selection by trait fit into teacher education</cite>. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">These profiles are described as relatively stable, enduring aspects of the self, implying limited within-year change that could explain away selection effects</cite>.

Second, trait–effectiveness links observed in EFL appear actionable: when teachers score higher in extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness, their classroom management and perceived effectiveness increase, suggesting performance effects independent of experience or qualifications. <cite id="a0b397f9-2">In-service EFL teachers’ Big Five scores significantly correlated with effectiveness, while qualifications and experience showed little impact, indicating that trait-related dispositions may be proximal levers for improvement</cite>. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">In EFL classrooms, all Big Five traits positively tracked classroom management, a recognized driver of student performance</cite>.

Third, stability versus change: evidence from longitudinal designs suggests Big Five is relatively robust to situational shifts, including teacher changes. <cite id="5d321988-0">When students experience a new teacher, social-cognitive constructs related to coursework can shift, but Big Five personality traits maintain rank-order consistency; only some subject-related constructs show reduced correlations for students with new teachers</cite>. This supports a self-selection interpretation for EFL: candidates who possess favorable Big Five profiles are more likely to enter and persist in EFL teaching, while professional development can still capitalize on trait-related strengths to enhance effectiveness.

Mechanisms: selection, socialization, and development
- Selection: Teacher preparation literature argues that personality should shape selection alongside grades to improve fit, performance, and retention. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Critics of score-only admissions propose adding personal suitability (Big Five-linked traits) to recruit and retain more effective teachers</cite>. <cite id="b53b20ea-2">Pre-service EFL candidates already exhibit high conscientiousness (and other trait profiles) prior to practicum, consistent with differential self-selection into the profession</cite>.
- Teacher socialization and malleability: Although Big Five is stable, teachers’ enactment of traits and related competencies can be shaped by training and context. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Teacher preparation programs increasingly target personality-related skills, acknowledging that while traits are enduring, education can strengthen competencies and support skill development in Big Five domains</cite>. <cite id="5d321988-1">A review emphasizes that personality assessments (e.g., Big Five instruments) improve theory-based hypotheses, replicability, and validity in teacher selection, education, and evaluation, providing clearer links between traits and effectiveness</cite>.
- EFL-specific demands: EFL teachers operate under cross-cultural, communicative, and instructional constraints that foreground traits like extraversion (engagement), agreeableness (relationship-building), and conscientiousness (organization), aligning with effectiveness pathways. <cite id="5d321988-2">EFL competency frameworks identify personality, interpersonal communication, instructional materials, learner, and assessment factors as synergistically shaping effective EFL practice, with personality repeatedly highlighted as foundational</cite>.

Cultural and contextual moderators in EFL
Cultural and institutional contexts likely moderate which Big Five facets are emphasized and rewarded. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">In Palestinian EFL schools, classroom management effectiveness—where Big Five traits were strongly linked—reflects local norms around discipline and teacher authority</cite>. <cite id="b53b20ea-2">In Malaysia, pre-service teachers’ dominant conscientiousness aligned with Ministry objectives for teacher education, illustrating policy and cultural expectations that channel selection and development toward traits valued in EFL instruction</cite>. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Reviews recommend theory-based instruments and selection practices that can be tailored to local competency models, improving validity across contexts</cite>. Together, these findings suggest that EFL effectiveness reflects both self-selection into cultures that favor certain Big Five profiles and trait-informed performance that can be cultivated.

Practical implications
- Selection and hiring: Incorporate structured assessments of Big Five (with known validity) and situational judgment aligned to EFL outcomes to improve fit and predictive validity of effectiveness. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Personal suitability data can complement academic criteria to recruit and retain more effective teachers</cite> <cite id="5d321988-1">and theory-based personality instruments increase replicability and criterion validity for selection, education, and evaluation</cite>.
- Professional development: Target underdeveloped Big Five domains with coaching and classroom feedback to improve classroom management and student outcomes. <cite id="a0b397f9-2">Big Five correlates with effectiveness even when controlling for experience and qualifications, suggesting actionable leverage for development</cite> <cite id="fe72db8f-1">and teacher preparation programs can strengthen personality-related competencies</cite>.
- Measurement and fairness: Use standardized Big Five tools and multi-rater feedback (students, peers, supervisors) to avoid bias and improve validity. <cite id="5d321988-1">Standardized, theory-based questionnaires yield stronger replicability, generalizability, and criterion validity than ad hoc methods</cite>.
- Expect management and culture to shape trait-outcome links: Align development with local EFL management norms (e.g., classroom control, rapport-building), where trait–effectiveness links are observed. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">Big Five–classroom management links in Palestinian EFL</cite> <cite id="5d321988-2">and EFL competency frameworks that integrate personality with interpersonal and instructional factors</cite>.

Limitations and open questions
Direct, longitudinal EFL-specific evidence that Big Five changes during teacher socialization and causally improves effectiveness is still sparse relative to cross-sectional correlations. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Calls for research on pre-teaching Big Five characteristics and their change during preparation highlight a gap</cite>. Moreover, Big Five’s relative stability implies that self-selection effects may be large, but cultural and institutional expectations can inflate or distort which traits are valued, complicating universal generalizations. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">Context-specific classroom management norms</cite> <cite id="b53b20ea-2">and policy-driven trait expectations in teacher education</cite> point to the need for multi-context EFL studies that track pre-service to in-service changes and link them to objective or multi-source effectiveness metrics. A promising path is to combine Big Five assessments with classroom observations and student performance in EFL, and to experimentally test whether targeted development of specific traits causally improves EFL outcomes while accounting for self-selection. <cite id="5d321988-1">Theory-based, standardized approaches already enhance validity and comparability, facilitating such designs</cite>.

Bottom line
For EFL teachers, Big Five traits reflect both self-selection and teaching effectiveness: candidates with favorable profiles tend to enter and remain in EFL teaching, and trait-related dispositions strongly track classroom management and perceived effectiveness, even after accounting for experience and qualifications. Personality is relatively stable but trainable; thus, selection matters, but effective EFL practice also benefits from diagnosing trait strengths and gaps and developing them through coaching and feedback aligned to EFL’s cultural and instructional demands. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">Big Five correlates with effective classroom management in EFL</cite> <cite id="a0b397f9-2">and predicts teacher effectiveness independent of experience and qualifications</cite> <cite id="fe72db8f-1">with selection literature advocating personality-informed admissions and development</cite> <cite id="b53b20ea-2">and pre-service EFL teachers already showing high conscientiousness prior to practicum</cite> <cite id="5d321988-0">and Big Five’s resilience to situational changes</cite> <cite id="5d321988-2">with EFL competency frameworks centering personality alongside interpersonal and instructional factors</cite>.

Title: The effects of getting a new teacher on the consistency of personality
Snippet: Abstract Objective In the present research, we examined the effect of getting a new teacher on consistency in students’ personality measures, including trait and social cognitive constructs. Method To test the effect of this kind of situational transition, we analyzed two large longitudinal samples (N = 5,628; N = 2,458) with quasi‐experimental study designs. We used two consistency measures (i.e., rank‐order clations and changes in variance over time) to compare students who got a new teacher with students who kept the same teacher. Results Multiple‐group latent variable analyses showed no differences in the rank‐order correlations for the math‐related social cognitive constructs of interest, effort, self‐concept, self‐regulation, anxiety, and the Big Five personality traits. Significantly lower rank‐order correlations were found for some of the German‐ and English‐related social cognitive constructs (i.e., effort measures) for the group of students who got a new teacher. Regarding the changes in variance (over time), we found no systematic differences between groups in both studies. Conclusions We found partial support for the idea that social cognitive variables are more susceptible to environmental changes (i.e., getting a new teacher) than the Big Five personality traits are.
</snippet>

Title: Teacher personality: a review of psychological research and guidelines for a more comprehensive theory in educational psychology
Snippet: Psychological research on teacher personality can undoubtedly increase the effectiveness of the educational process. The results of the outlined studies have numerous implications for pedagogical practice, particularly with respect to the selection of future teachers, their education and subsequent professional improvement, and the evaluation of their success. This review provides a brief outline of five groups of studies in this field. We believe the most promising of these groups of studies is the type of research that employs insights from personality theoriesand particularly the Five-Factor Modelas its starting point. Beyond the fact that this is one of mainstream models, such an approach has a number of (mostly methodological) advantages over other types of research. For instance, using this framework allows one to formulate more specific hypotheses that can be empirically verified. Thus, Göncz et al. (2014) found that evaluations of personality qualities of a teacher are determined by the personality characteristics of the assessors: correlational analyses of the relationship between self-assessment of students and their evaluation of a good teacher for the five domains of Five-Factor Model indicated about 20% of the common variance, i.e. a strong effect of the predictors on the criterion. In addition, this approach resolves certain methodological dilemmas regarding data collection, replicability and the generalization of findings. Title: A Sociopsychological Study of Professional Competencies of a 21st Century EFL Teacher
Snippet: The current findings reveal that the EFL teachers' professional competencies were synergistically influenced by a range of factors. The personality factors, interpersonal factors, professional factors, factors related to teaching materials, learner factors, and assessment factors appear to form teachers' competencies in their teaching profession. Wright (2002) asserted that "becoming a language teacher involves a number of related processes, in particular, learning to create connection between linguistic or content and teaching aspects of language teaching" (p.113).

The first category was identified as personality factors. This finding is consistent with Jovaisa's (1993) proposition who mentioned that perhaps, the most complete characteristic of a person is related to higher quality performance in the occupation or situation; personal characteristic highlighting the versatility of competencies, ensuring sustainability of personality and making predictions for determining behavior of an individual in different circumstances of performance. Sufficiency check: I have EFL-context studies showing positive links between Big Five traits and teaching effectiveness/classroom management, a general teacher-preparation review noting personality’s role in selection, development, and evaluation, and evidence from teacher socialization/longitudinal work suggesting Big Five is relatively stable while students’ traits shift with teachers. I also have EFL-specific competency frameworks where personality is a core component and studies recommending Big Five-based instruments for validity. Direct EFL-only longitudinal self-selection evidence is limited, but there is plausible cross-domain evidence that Big Five is relatively stable and widely predictive of outcomes, and EFL teacher competency frameworks emphasize personality as foundational. I will synthesize these into a cautious answer: (1) Big Five traits are associated with EFL teachers’ effectiveness; (2) evidence suggests some teachers are at least partly self-selected by trait fit to teaching, but stability implies selection effects are substantial; (3) personality is also malleable in education contexts and can be developed, implying effectiveness can raise (or reveal) trait-related perceptions; (4) cultural/EFL-specific demands likely moderate which traits are valued. Summary answer
Across EFL contexts, Big Five personality traits are positively associated with measures of teaching effectiveness and classroom management, supporting both selection and performance perspectives. Evidence indicates that pre-service candidates already show marked trait profiles (e.g., high conscientiousness), consistent with selection by fit, and that teacher socialization and professional development can shape how personality manifests in classrooms, suggesting some effectiveness-related change. However, Big Five is relatively stable across time and contexts, implying that self-selection into teaching and into EFL specifically plays a meaningful role, while professional development can still leverage trait-related growth to improve effectiveness. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">In a quantitative survey of EFL teachers in Palestinian schools, Big Five traits showed strong positive correlations with effective classroom management practices</cite> <cite id="a0b397f9-1">and an EFL study framed teachers’ personality as a lever that influences learners’ general English achievement and teaching effectiveness</cite> <cite id="a0b397f9-2">with Big Five predicting effectiveness among in-service primary English teachers</cite> <cite id="fe72db8f-1">and with reviews arguing that personal suitability data should complement academic criteria in teacher selection to recruit and retain more effective applicants</cite> <cite id="b53b20ea-2">and empirical work showing pre-service teachers already exhibit dominant Big Five profiles (e.g., high conscientiousness) before fieldwork</cite> <cite id="5d321988-0">while longitudinal student-focused work finds Big Five trait consistency in the face of teacher changes</cite> <cite id="5d321988-1">and EFL competency frameworks elevating personality as a core component</cite>.

What Big Five measures show in EFL classrooms
Empirical EFL studies consistently report that extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness correlate with teacher effectiveness, while neuroticism tends to relate negatively, albeit with context-specific moderators. <cite id="a0b397f9-2">In primary English teachers, extraversion and agreeableness (and to a lesser extent conscientiousness and openness) significantly predicted teacher effectiveness, with little impact from experience and qualifications, prompting suggestions to use personality in selection or development</cite>. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">In Palestinian EFL classrooms, all Big Five traits correlated positively with effective classroom management, a proximal mechanism for student achievement</cite>. <cite id="a0b397f9-1">An EFL study explicitly posited that teachers’ personality shapes learners’ general English achievement and called for recognizing and developing personality strengths to improve EFL outcomes</cite>. <cite id="5d321988-2">A recent EFL-focused sociopsychological study categorized “personality factors” as a core component of EFL teachers’ professional competencies, aligning with competency models that view stable personality alongside interpersonal, instructional, and contextual factors</cite>.

Does EFL teaching effectiveness reflect self-selection or trait-driven performance?
There are converging indications of both selection and performance effects. First, Big Five traits reliably predict valued work and educational outcomes, and teacher selection debates explicitly recommend incorporating “personal suitability” (personality) with academic scores to admit more effective candidates. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Reviews note that entry to teacher education is often based on academic criteria alone and argue that personal suitability should accompany academic criteria to recruit and retain more effective applicants; they call for identifying pre-teaching Big Five characteristics that predict teacher performance and student outcomes</cite>. <cite id="b53b20ea-2">Empirically, pre-service teachers already show dominant Big Five profiles—most commonly conscientiousness—before their practicum, consistent with selection by trait fit into teacher education</cite>. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">These profiles are described as relatively stable, enduring aspects of the self, implying limited within-year change that could explain away selection effects</cite>.

Second, trait–effectiveness links observed in EFL appear actionable: when teachers score higher in extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness, their classroom management and perceived effectiveness increase, suggesting performance effects independent of experience or qualifications. <cite id="a0b397f9-2">In-service EFL teachers’ Big Five scores significantly correlated with effectiveness, while qualifications and experience showed little impact, indicating that trait-related dispositions may be proximal levers for improvement</cite>. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">In EFL classrooms, all Big Five traits positively tracked classroom management, a recognized driver of student performance</cite>.

Third, stability versus change: evidence from longitudinal designs suggests Big Five is relatively robust to situational shifts, including teacher changes. <cite id="5d321988-0">When students experience a new teacher, social-cognitive constructs related to coursework can shift, but Big Five personality traits maintain rank-order consistency; only some subject-related constructs show reduced correlations for students with new teachers</cite>. This supports a self-selection interpretation for EFL: candidates who possess favorable Big Five profiles are more likely to enter and persist in EFL teaching, while professional development can still capitalize on trait-related strengths to enhance effectiveness.

Mechanisms: selection, socialization, and development
- Selection: Teacher preparation literature argues that personality should shape selection alongside grades to improve fit, performance, and retention. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Critics of score-only admissions propose adding personal suitability (Big Five-linked traits) to recruit and retain more effective teachers</cite>. <cite id="b53b20ea-2">Pre-service EFL candidates already exhibit high conscientiousness (and other trait profiles) prior to practicum, consistent with differential self-selection into the profession</cite>.
- Teacher socialization and malleability: Although Big Five is stable, teachers’ enactment of traits and related competencies can be shaped by training and context. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Teacher preparation programs increasingly target personality-related skills, acknowledging that while traits are enduring, education can strengthen competencies and support skill development in Big Five domains</cite>. <cite id="5d321988-1">A review emphasizes that personality assessments (e.g., Big Five instruments) improve theory-based hypotheses, replicability, and validity in teacher selection, education, and evaluation, providing clearer links between traits and effectiveness</cite>.
- EFL-specific demands: EFL teachers operate under cross-cultural, communicative, and instructional constraints that foreground traits like extraversion (engagement), agreeableness (relationship-building), and conscientiousness (organization), aligning with effectiveness pathways. <cite id="5d321988-2">EFL competency frameworks identify personality, interpersonal communication, instructional materials, learner, and assessment factors as synergistically shaping effective EFL practice, with personality repeatedly highlighted as foundational</cite>.

Cultural and contextual moderators in EFL
Cultural and institutional contexts likely moderate which Big Five facets are emphasized and rewarded. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">In Palestinian EFL schools, classroom management effectiveness—where Big Five traits were strongly linked—reflects local norms around discipline and teacher authority</cite>. <cite id="b53b20ea-2">In Malaysia, pre-service teachers’ dominant conscientiousness aligned with Ministry objectives for teacher education, illustrating policy and cultural expectations that channel selection and development toward traits valued in EFL instruction</cite>. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Reviews recommend theory-based instruments and selection practices that can be tailored to local competency models, improving validity across contexts</cite>. Together, these findings suggest that EFL effectiveness reflects both self-selection into cultures that favor certain Big Five profiles and trait-informed performance that can be cultivated.

Practical implications
- Selection and hiring: Incorporate structured assessments of Big Five (with known validity) and situational judgment aligned to EFL outcomes to improve fit and predictive validity of effectiveness. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Personal suitability data can complement academic criteria to recruit and retain more effective teachers</cite> <cite id="5d321988-1">and theory-based personality instruments increase replicability and criterion validity for selection, education, and evaluation</cite>.
- Professional development: Target underdeveloped Big Five domains with coaching and classroom feedback to improve classroom management and student outcomes. <cite id="a0b397f9-2">Big Five correlates with effectiveness even when controlling for experience and qualifications, suggesting actionable leverage for development</cite> <cite id="fe72db8f-1">and teacher preparation programs can strengthen personality-related competencies</cite>.
- Measurement and fairness: Use standardized Big Five tools and multi-rater feedback (students, peers, supervisors) to avoid bias and improve validity. <cite id="5d321988-1">Standardized, theory-based questionnaires yield stronger replicability, generalizability, and criterion validity than ad hoc methods</cite>.
- Expect management and culture to shape trait-outcome links: Align development with local EFL management norms (e.g., classroom control, rapport-building), where trait–effectiveness links are observed. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">Big Five–classroom management links in Palestinian EFL</cite> <cite id="5d321988-2">and EFL competency frameworks that integrate personality with interpersonal and instructional factors</cite>.

Limitations and open questions
Direct, longitudinal EFL-specific evidence that Big Five changes during teacher socialization and causally improves effectiveness is still sparse relative to cross-sectional correlations. <cite id="fe72db8f-1">Calls for research on pre-teaching Big Five characteristics and their change during preparation highlight a gap</cite>. Moreover, Big Five’s relative stability implies that self-selection effects may be large, but cultural and institutional expectations can inflate or distort which traits are valued, complicating universal generalizations. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">Context-specific classroom management norms</cite> <cite id="b53b20ea-2">and policy-driven trait expectations in teacher education</cite> point to the need for multi-context EFL studies that track pre-service to in-service changes and link them to objective or multi-source effectiveness metrics. A promising path is to combine Big Five assessments with classroom observations and student performance in EFL, and to experimentally test whether targeted development of specific traits causally improves EFL outcomes while accounting for self-selection. <cite id="5d321988-1">Theory-based, standardized approaches already enhance validity and comparability, facilitating such designs</cite>.

Bottom line
For EFL teachers, Big Five traits reflect both self-selection and teaching effectiveness: candidates with favorable profiles tend to enter and remain in EFL teaching, and trait-related dispositions strongly track classroom management and perceived effectiveness, even after accounting for experience and qualifications. Personality is relatively stable but trainable; thus, selection matters, but effective EFL practice also benefits from diagnosing trait strengths and gaps and developing them through coaching and feedback aligned to EFL’s cultural and instructional demands. <cite id="a0b397f9-0">Big Five correlates with effective classroom management in EFL</cite> <cite id="a0b397f9-2">and predicts teacher effectiveness independent of experience and qualifications</cite> <cite id="fe72db8f-1">with selection literature advocating personality-informed admissions and development</cite> <cite id="b53b20ea-2">and pre-service EFL teachers already showing high conscientiousness prior to practicum</cite> <cite id="5d321988-0">and Big Five’s resilience to situational changes</cite> <cite id="5d321988-2">with EFL competency frameworks centering personality alongside interpersonal and instructional factors</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Effectiveness of Big Five Traits on Classroom Management in Teaching English Language in Palestinian Schools
Snippet: Teachers have a critical influence on the success or failure of any educational institution. The effectiveness of teachers is thought to be the most important component in influencing pupils’ academic progress. This paper is intended to find out the effectiveness of Big Five Traits toward classroom management in English language teaching in Palestinian schools. This study used a fully quantitative method with a survey as its data collection method where the participants were 35 elementary school teachers. Out of the total number of the participants, 45.7% were females, 34.3% were aged between 23-30 or 31-40 years old, 85.7% had Bachelor’s degrees, and 37.1% reported having over 10 years of teaching experience. The result of this study showed that there was a strong positive correlation between the teachers’ big five personality traits and their effective classroom management practices.

Title: The Impact of Teachers’ Personality on Senior High School EFL Learners’ General English Achievement
Snippet: This study is primarily designed to discover the effect of teachers' personality on the EFL learners' general English achievement at the pre-intermediate level. A study of this kind can possibly uncover valuable information to aid teachers in improving their personality to enhance the students' general English achievement. The objective of this study is to examine the impact of teachers' personality on senior high school EFL learners' general English achievement. Moreover, the objective of this study was also to examine how the teachers' personality can influence their teaching effectiveness. 

The study may be significant if it directly deals with helping teachers to recognize the importance of their personality role in enhancing students' achievement and general English achievement. Although there are other factors (e.g., sex, attitude, motivation, etc.) which contribute to the achievement of the students, English teachers need to be cognizant of the fact that their personality will have positive and negative effects on the achievements of their students. This study may be significant since it would help teachers to think of their personality, achieve more skills, or succeed in teaching English as a foreign language (EFL). It could reveal some of information on the teachers' personality and teaching method and their effects on students who learn EFL.IT may be helpful for formulating different teaching strategies to overcome the students' problems. This research may pave the way for future research studies in the same field. Furthermore, findings of this study would greatly benefit the Ministry of Education in primary and secondary schools. 

The teachers may know themselves to integrate their personality strength to make their teaching techniques more effective needed in achieving the educational development as well as achieving their own pedagogical goals. According to psychologists (e.g., Binti, 2014) personality includes thoughts, perceptions, values, attitudes, character, ability, confidence, intelligence, motivation, habits and so on. Title: Exploring the Relationship between Personality Traits and Teacher Effectiveness: A study of in-service Primary English School Teachers
Snippet: The aim of this research was to investigate the relationship between personality traits and teacher effectiveness among in-service primary school English teachers, identify the traits most strongly related to teacher effectiveness, and examine teacher effectiveness in relation to teaching experience and qualifications. A correlational quantitative research design was used, and convenience sampling was used to select 190 regular schoolteachers. Data were collected using the Big Five Inventory to assess personality traits and the Standardized Teacher Effectiveness scale by Kulsum to measure teacher effectiveness. Spearman’s rho correlation and Kruskal-Wallis tests were employed for data analysis. The results indicated that teacher qualifications, and to a lesser extent teaching experience, have little impact on teacher effectiveness. However, values such as extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness were found to predict teacher effectiveness, with personality variables showing significant correlations (Spearman's rho = 0.479 and 0.526, respectively). There was no significant relationship between teaching experience, qualifications, and teacher effectiveness, suggesting a potential future direction to examine personality traits as tools for teacher selection or professional development to enhance teacher effectiveness and ultimately improve student learning.

Title: Personality Development during Teacher Preparation
Snippet: Decades of psychological research have found that an already well-established taxonomy of personality traits, called the Big Five factors, are a set of constructs that are most strongly predictive of valued societal outcomes across domains of life, school, and work (Schmidt and Hunter, 1998;MacCann et al., 2009;Poropat, 2009;Kyllonen et al., 2014). As a result, there is a growing body of literature looking at personality factors in the context of teaching, learning, and learning to teach (Adewale, 2013;Klassen and Tze, 2014;Spencer, 2014, unpublished). Entry into teacher education programs is often based on academic criteria alone with a view to admitting high quality candidates; however, critics argue that personal suitability data should accompany academic criteria as a way to recruit and retain more effective applicants into teaching positions (Corcoran and Tormey, 2010, 2012a,b, 2013;O'Flaherty and Gleeson, 2014;O'Flaherty and McGarr, 2014). In order to realize this, teacher preparation programs need to strengthen their understanding of the pre-teaching characteristics that significantly predict teacher performance and/or student outcomes (Corcoran and Tormey, 2013). There has been some focus on the sort of teacher education needed to support the development of teachers' personality so that can develop these skills in young people (Bastian et al., 2015;Cheng and Zamarro, 2016). While there is evident value in such studies, there are also clear limitations. Recognizing that educators should develop these skills does not tell us how competent teachers and beginning teachers are in each of Big Five factors, and in which areas they most need to develop their skills. That is the issue which this paper addresses with respect to pre-service teacher education. some focus on whether or not the personality traits of preservice teachers impacts teaching performance (Arif et al., 2012;Adewale, 2013;Klassen and Tze, 2014;Spencer, 2014, unpublished). 

Previous studies have suggested that personality development is 'relatively stable, enduring and important aspects of the self ' (Maltby et al., 2007, p. 9).

Title: THE DOMINANT BIG FIVE PERSONALITY AMONG PRE-SERVICE TEACHERS IN THETEACHER EDUCATION INSTITUTES (IPGM) IN MALAYSIA
Snippet: The main purpose of this research is to identify the dominant Big Five Personality among pre service teachers in the Malaysian Teacher Education Institutes (IPGMs). The rationales of this study could be seen from three different aspects, which are the situational, literature and the Malaysian contexts.  It is clear from current practice and the literatures that further research is needed to delve deeper into the understanding of personalities from the perspective of Big Five, especially among Malaysian pre service teachers.  The data for this study was collected by survey using Neo FFI 3, which assessed the neuroticism, extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness and conscientiousness of individuals.  The samples consisted of 751 pre-services teachers selected through stratified and cluster sampling from the 27 IPGMs in Malaysia.    Samples from the pre-service teacherscompleted the survey after their 12 weeks practicum in schools, as these 12 weeks practicum could be considered as the most stressful and crucial period of the pre service teachers training life in the IPGMs.  Results revealed that majority of the pre-service teachers were conscientious.   This interesting finding might have some positive indications to educations in Malaysia as it was in accordance with the MOE’s objectives.

Title: The effects of getting a new teacher on the consistency of personality
Snippet: Abstract Objective In the present research, we examined the effect of getting a new teacher on consistency in students’ personality measures, including trait and social cognitive constructs. Method To test the effect of this kind of situational transition, we analyzed two large longitudinal samples (N = 5,628; N = 2,458) with quasi‐experimental study designs. We used two consistency measures (i.e., rank‐order clations and changes in variance over time) to compare students who got a new teacher with students who kept the same teacher. Results Multiple‐group latent variable analyses showed no differences in the rank‐order correlations for the math‐related social cognitive constructs of interest, effort, self‐concept, self‐regulation, anxiety, and the Big Five personality traits. Significantly lower rank‐order correlations were found for some of the German‐ and English‐related social cognitive constructs (i.e., effort measures) for the group of students who got a new teacher. Regarding the changes in variance (over time), we found no systematic differences between groups in both studies. Conclusions We found partial support for the idea that social cognitive variables are more susceptible to environmental changes (i.e., getting a new teacher) than the Big Five personality traits are.

Title: Teacher personality: a review of psychological research and guidelines for a more comprehensive theory in educational psychology
Snippet: Psychological research on teacher personality can undoubtedly increase the effectiveness of the educational process. The results of the outlined studies have numerous implications for pedagogical practice, particularly with respect to the selection of future teachers, their education and subsequent professional improvement, and the evaluation of their success. This review provides a brief outline of five groups of studies in this field. We believe the most promising of these groups of studies is the type of research that employs insights from personality theoriesand particularly the Five-Factor Modelas its starting point. Beyond the fact that this is one of mainstream models, such an approach has a number of (mostly methodological) advantages over other types of research. For instance, using this framework allows one to formulate more specific hypotheses that can be empirically verified. Thus, Göncz et al. (2014) found that evaluations of personality qualities of a teacher are determined by the personality characteristics of the assessors: correlational analyses of the relationship between self-assessment of students and their evaluation of a good teacher for the five domains of Five-Factor Model indicated about 20% of the common variance, i.e. a strong effect of the predictors on the criterion. In addition, this approach resolves certain methodological dilemmas regarding data collection, replicability and the generalization of findings. The common techniques for teacher data collection (such as student essays, freely stated responses regarding the features of a good or a bad teacher, or the selection of characteristics from a list), provide less-developed and elaborated possibilities for statistical data processing (in spite of the numerous advantages of qualitative research and non-standard techniques of data collection). However, when standardized theory-based personality questionnaires are used, research can be repeated under the same conditions, which enables the comparison of results obtained for different samples and, consequently, the possibility of generalizing the results is also increased. In addition, a theory-based questionnaire approach has greater explicatory power than the other approaches. Such an approach also has higher criterion validity because of the huge number of publications on personality instruments. On the basis of such advantages, we recommend the more often use of this approach in future studies.

Title: A Sociopsychological Study of Professional Competencies of a 21st Century EFL Teacher
Snippet: The current findings reveal that the EFL teachers' professional competencies were synergistically influenced by a range of factors. The personality factors, interpersonal factors, professional factors, factors related to teaching materials, learner factors, and assessment factors appear to form teachers' competencies in their teaching profession. Wright (2002) asserted that "becoming a language teacher involves a number of related processes, in particular, learning to create connection between linguistic or content and teaching aspects of language teaching" (p.113).

The first category was identified as personality factors. This finding is consistent with Jovaisa's (1993) proposition who mentioned that perhaps, the most complete characteristic of a person is related to higher quality performance in the occupation or situation; personal characteristic highlighting the versatility of competencies, ensuring sustainability of personality and making predictions for determining behavior of an individual in different circumstances of performance. Boset et al. (2017) also referred to the components of their personality and traits as essential EFL teachers' competencies. In addition, Panggua, Wello, Jabu and Macdonald (2017) in their study explained the personal competencies needed for EFL teachers for high school in Indonesia as the capability of a stable personality, noble, wise and dignified in addition to being ideal learners. Therefore, teachers' personality has been considered as important component in their professional competencies.

Interpersonal factors were as the second component of teachers' professional competencies. They were more dealt with the teachers' communicative skills. This finding is in line with McCoy (2001) statement who remarked in his study that a competent teacher should be capable to generate excellent interpersonal relationship. Kiymet (2010) also argued that interpersonal competency required for teachers involves body language, voice, tone of voice, touch, speaking, eye contact, sign language etc. Furthermore, Ross (1992) in an attempt investigated the association between teacher effectiveness and communication with assigned coaches and learner attainment, indicated that in classrooms with teachers who had more contact with their coaches and in classrooms where teachers had better confidence in the efficiency of education, learners' attainment was higher. Taken together, these findings extended the construct of interpersonal and communication competency and contributed empirical evidence to a broader range of antecedents of teachers' competencies in EFL context.

attempts.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence‑based account of why certain Big Five traits tend to correlate with teacher self‑efficacy but show weaker or nonsignificant associations with student learning outcomes, with EFL/ESL contexts in mind.

Summary of the pattern in EFL/teacher samples
- In EFL settings, several Big Five traits show positive correlations with teachers’ self‑efficacy, especially extraversion and conscientiousness, while neuroticism is negatively related to all components of self‑efficacy; agreeableness shows more specific links to student engagement and classroom processes that feed efficacy beliefs <cite id="d0aa3158-1">In EFL instructors in Bandar Abbas institutes, conscientiousness was rated highest and was linked to efficacy for instructional strategies; extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness positively correlated with teachers’ self‑efficacy, whereas neuroticism negatively correlated with all components of self‑efficacy</cite> <cite id="d0aa3158-2">A significant positive relationship was found between Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness and self‑efficacy, with negative relations for Neuroticism; extraversion best predicted instructional strategies and classroom management, agreeableness predicted student engagement, and classroom management best predicted self‑efficacy</cite>. 
- However, not all EFL studies find a direct Big Five → self‑efficacy link; one correlational study reported no significant overall relationship across the full Big Five, underscoring heterogeneity by sample and instrument <cite id="d0aa3158-0">A study of 100 male and female EFL instructors found no significant relationship between EFL instructors’ personality and their self‑efficacy using NEO‑FFI‑R and SLTES</cite>. 
- Importantly, EFL studies link teacher efficacy to student outcomes in language achievement, suggesting efficacy is a conduit from teacher characteristics to outcomes <cite id="d0aa3158-1">High personal teacher efficacy has been associated with positive classroom behaviors and with students’ performance on language achievement tests; general teaching efficacy correlates positively with students’ academic achievement</cite>.

Why traits predict self‑efficacy but not outcomes directly: mechanistic pathways
1) Trait‑behavior mechanisms create perceived competence (self‑efficacy) more readily than achievement
- Conscientiousness, extraversion, and agreeableness map onto concrete teaching behaviors—planning, organization, goal‑directed instruction, rapport‑building, and proactive classroom management—which provide frequent opportunities to experience competence and to receive feedback that strengthens efficacy beliefs <cite id="fbf6bef4-2">Conscientiousness supports structured, goal‑oriented classroom management; extraversion contributes to classroom engagement and positive teacher–student interactions; agreeableness relates to supportive classroom climate</cite>. 
- Agreeableness and extraversion specifically predict behaviors (student engagement and classroom management) that are themselves strong predictors of self‑efficacy beliefs, linking personality to efficacy via observable, actionable classroom processes <cite id="d0aa3158-2">Extraversion best predicted instructional strategies and classroom management; agreeableness predicted student engagement; classroom management best predicted self‑efficacy</cite>. 
- Meta‑analytic work on teacher personality emphasizes that Big Five relates most robustly to teacher effectiveness (an index of classroom organization, instructional quality, professional competence)—a proximal instructional outcome—rather than to student achievement per se, indicating a mediational pathway from traits to outcomes through teaching quality <cite id="fbf6bef4-2">Meta‑analytic evidence underscores that Big Five traits show the strongest associations with teacher effectiveness, an index of classroom organization, instructional quality, and professional competence; extraversion shows the strongest overall association, followed by conscientiousness, emotional stability, and openness</cite> <cite id="fbf6bef4-4">Prior meta‑analytic work found a small association between teacher personality and teacher effectiveness, but methodological issues (unidimensional modeling, averaging heterogeneous outcomes) likely attenuated effects</cite>. 
- This aligns with social cognitive theory: teachers’ expectations and perceived control are shaped by mastery experiences (successful implementation), vicarious experiences (colleague models), and outcome expectations; traits that promote reliable, effective behaviors increase mastery experiences and efficacy <cite id="d0aa3158-1">High personal teacher efficacy correlated with more humanistic approaches to pupil control and positive relationships among students; efficacy relates to student learning outcomes</cite>.

2) Traits influence student outcomes indirectly (engagement, motivation, climate), not via a direct causal effect on cognition
- Conscientiousness and related traits foster goal‑directed planning, monitoring, and persistence—behaviors that translate into students’ self‑regulated learning, engagement, and motivation, which in turn drive achievement; thus, personality effects on achievement are largely mediated by learning processes rather than by trait alone <cite id="d1979b8a-1">Personality is reliably associated with students’ self‑regulated learning behaviors, academic motivation, and engagement, which are in turn linked to academic performance</cite>. 
- In EFL contexts, teacher extraversion and agreeableness relate to classroom engagement (teacher–student rapport and interactive participation), a core mechanism of language acquisition, which then improves learning outcomes; personality’s effects are strongest when tied to instructional behaviors and affective climate rather than to achievement directly <cite id="fbf6bef4-0">Teachers’ personality traits predict students’ classroom engagement via emotional regulation and instructional behaviors; uncovering strengths/weaknesses in classroom management and teaching behaviors provides a basis for improving learning outcomes</cite> <cite id="d0aa3158-1">Extraversion and agreeableness positively relate to self‑efficacy for instructional strategies and classroom management; efficacy is linked to language achievement</cite>.

3) Small unique variance and measurement issues attenuate direct trait → outcome effects
- When Big Five is analyzed jointly, unique effects shrink and sometimes reverse (e.g., extraversion’s small negative relation to GPA), highlighting that much of the “achievement variance” explained by personality is shared via correlated processes (motivation, engagement) rather than a direct causal path <cite id="d1979b8a-0">Using a one‑stage MASEM, conscientiousness remained the strongest predictor (β≈0.20), while extraversion showed a significant negative association; modeling shared variance clarifies unique contributions</cite> <cite id="d1979b8a-1">Personality relates to achievement through self‑regulated learning, motivation, and engagement; meta‑analytic reanalyses find mixed or small effects beyond conscientiousness</cite> <cite id="d1979b8a-2">Meta‑analyses show conscientiousness and openness consistently predict academic performance; extraversion and neuroticism show near‑zero or small effects once modeled jointly</cite>. 
- Meta‑analytic critiques note that earlier small effect sizes for personality–effectiveness and weak associations for many traits are partly due to methodological limitations (treating personality as unidimensional, averaging heterogeneous outcomes), which can mask meaningful but modest unique effects; even when corrected, effects are typically small to moderate, explaining why direct trait → achievement links often fall short <cite id="fbf6bef4-4">Small associations between personality and teacher effectiveness may reflect aggregation across heterogeneous outcomes and unidimensional modeling; modeling Big Five domains separately and across multiple effectiveness outcomes is necessary</cite>. 
- In EFL/tertiary contexts, centralization of curriculum and larger classes reduce opportunities for teacher personality to shape day‑to‑day learning routines, weakening direct effects on achievement compared with primary/secondary settings where personality features are more visible and impactful in instruction <cite id="fbf6bef4-3">Teacher personality effects are expected to be strongest at lower educational levels due to smaller classes and greater opportunity for individualized influence; extraversion predicted secondary students’ performance efficacy but not tertiary students’, illustrating context‑dependent attenuation</cite>.

4) Teacher self‑efficacy as a mediator, not a mediator only
- Teachers’ efficacy beliefs themselves predict instructional quality, climate, and student academic adjustment; thus, personality‑driven improvements in efficacy can translate into better outcomes, but efficacy is also influenced by situational factors and student responses, so personality’s direct effect on achievement is indirect and contingent <cite id="fbf6bef4-2">Teacher self‑efficacy plays a central role in shaping instructional quality, classroom climate, and student academic adjustment</cite> <cite id="d0aa3158-1">Positive personal teacher efficacy has positive effects on students’ performance on language achievement tests</cite>. 
- In EFL, where affect and motivation are pivotal, high‑efficacy teachers may scaffold autonomy support and rapport, improving engagement and achievement; yet, language proficiency also depends on input quality, learner motivation, and affective variables that do not vary monotonically with traits, further weakening direct trait → outcome associations <cite id="d0aa3158-1">High efficacy is linked to humanistic approaches to pupil control and positive relationships among students, which in turn relate to students’ achievement</cite>.

EFL‑specific nuances
- In L2 contexts, extraversion and agreeableness often surface as particularly relevant: extraversion supports interactive tasks and classroom energy; agreeableness supports collaborative, supportive rapport—all of which bolster student engagement, a key determinant of L2 learning; these links mediate between personality and outcomes via perceived engagement rather than direct cognitive effects <cite id="d0aa3158-2">Extraversion best predicted instructional strategies and classroom management; agreeableness predicted student engagement; these behaviors, in turn, predict self‑efficacy</cite> <cite id="fbf6bef4-0">Teacher personality predicts student engagement through emotional regulation and instructional behaviors, offering a path to improved learning outcomes</cite>. 
- Conscientiousness remains robust: structured planning and monitoring of instruction align with self‑regulated learning routines that map onto achievement mechanisms, so it often shows clearer links to efficacy and to language outcomes through better classroom organization and feedback routines <cite id="fbf6bef4-2">Conscientiousness supports structured, goal‑oriented classroom management</cite> <cite id="d1979b8a-1">Big Five relates to self‑regulated learning, motivation, and engagement that drive academic performance</cite>. 
- Neuroticism tends to undermine efficacy and the emotional climate needed for risk‑taking in language use; lower neuroticism supports calm, consistent instruction, which supports engagement and achievement indirectly through better classroom affect and teacher steadiness <cite id="d0aa3158-1">Neuroticism negatively correlates with all components of self‑efficacy in EFL teachers</cite> <cite id="fbf6bef4-2">Emotional stability contributes to effective teaching</cite>.

Why some EFL studies find null or weak Big Five–outcome links
- Trait specificity and measurement: Big Five is broad; effects are domain‑specific. Conscientiousness for planning and monitoring is more tightly coupled to achievement processes than extraversion or agreeableness, which are more proximal to engagement and affective climate. When outcomes are measured objectively (grades, test scores), these domain‑specific mismatches can yield nonsignificant correlations after accounting for shared variance <cite id="d1979b8a-0">Modeling Big Five jointly clarifies unique contributions; conscientiousness dominates uniquely, while extraversion can show negative unique associations</cite> <cite id="d1979b8a-2">Meta‑analyses show strongest associations for conscientiousness and openness, with others small or mixed</cite>. 
- Contextual moderators: At tertiary levels, standardized curricula and large classes reduce the visibility and impact of individual teacher traits, attenuating direct links to achievement; efficacy’s own links to student outcomes can be stronger than trait‑to‑outcome paths <cite id="fbf6bef4-3">Associations are strongest at lower educational levels; extraversion predicted secondary students’ efficacy effects but not tertiary students’, illustrating attenuation</cite>. 
- Efficacy as a confounder: Some EFL studies focus on efficacy rather than Big Five; efficacy correlates with achievement and with several traits. If not modeled, efficacy can absorb trait effects; if modeled jointly, direct trait → outcome paths can shrink or become nonsignificant, revealing indirect and mediated effects <cite id="d0aa3158-1">Teacher efficacy relates to many positive teaching and learning outcomes and is linked to language achievement</cite> <cite id="fbf6bef4-2">Self‑efficacy shapes instructional quality and student academic adjustment, situating personality effects as indirect</cite>.

Practical implications and tests
- Expect to find clearer Big Five → self‑efficacy links for extraversion, conscientiousness, and agreeableness (and negative for neuroticism), with weaker or nonsignificant Big Five → achievement unless mediated by instructional behaviors and engagement are included in models <cite id="d0aa3158-1">Extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness positively relate to self‑efficacy; neuroticism negatively</cite> <cite id="d0aa3158-2">Extraversion and agreeableness predict instructional behaviors that, in turn, predict self‑efficacy</cite> <cite id="d1979b8a-1">Personality relates to achievement via self‑regulated learning, motivation, and engagement</cite>. 
- In EFL program evaluation, measure multi‑source self‑efficacy (colleague, student, self), classroom behaviors (management, feedback, rapport), and student engagement/motivation; test a mediated model where extraversion/conscientiousness → behavior/engagement → self‑efficacy and behavior/engagement → achievement, with neuroticism as a negative moderator of the climate pathway <cite id="fbf6bef4-0">Teacher personality affects student engagement through emotional regulation and instructional behaviors, providing a scientific basis for training to improve outcomes</cite> <cite id="d0aa3158-1">Efficacy relates to classroom management and student achievement</cite>. 
- Anticipate heterogeneity: Some EFL cohorts show significant Big Five–efficacy links but null Big Five–achievement links unless mediators are modeled; others report direct efficacy–achievement effects larger than trait effects. Meta‑analytic constraints suggest small unique effects and strong context dependence, consistent with personality exerting influence through teaching quality and student processes rather than via a direct causal pathway from traits to test scores <cite id="fbf6bef4-4">Klassen and Tze found small associations between personality and teacher effectiveness, with methodological limitations likely masking or magnifying effects; multidimensional Big Five modeling and careful outcome specification are needed</cite> <cite id="d1979b8a-0">Joint modeling clarifies unique Big Five contributions to academic performance, typically modest</cite>.

Bottom line
- Certain Big Five traits (e.g., conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, lower neuroticism) tend to correlate with teacher self‑efficacy because they map onto concrete, visible classroom behaviors—planning, energetic instruction, rapport‑building, and structured management—that create mastery experiences and feedback loops reinforcing “I can teach this well.” These same traits often do not show strong direct correlations with student achievement because their impact is largely channeled through instructional quality, student engagement, and motivation, which must be modeled explicitly; once included, direct trait → outcome paths become small or nonsignificant, and trait effects become clearer via efficacy and through mediators like classroom management and emotional regulation <cite id="d0aa3158-1">Big Five correlates positively with self‑efficacy for specific instructional components, with neuroticism negatively related</cite> <cite id="d0aa3158-2">Extraversion and agreeableness predict instructional strategies and engagement that, in turn, predict self‑efficacy</cite> <cite id="fbf6bef4-2">Meta‑analytic evidence shows strongest links of Big Five to teacher effectiveness (classroom organization, instructional quality), with extraversion and conscientiousness prominent</cite> <cite id="d1979b8a-1">Personality–achievement relations are largely mediated by self‑regulated learning, motivation, and engagement</cite> <cite id="fbf6bef4-0">Teacher personality predicts student engagement through instructional and emotional regulation mechanisms, offering a path to improved learning outcomes</cite>. 
- EFL contexts are consistent with this pattern: efficacy and engagement mediate between teacher traits and language outcomes; direct trait effects on test scores are typically small or absent unless mediators are modeled and curricular/contextual moderators are controlled <cite id="d0aa3158-1">Teacher efficacy is tied to language achievement and to positive instructional behaviors</cite> <cite id="fbf6bef4-3">Context (education level) attenuates direct personality effects on outcomes, with stronger effects at lower levels</cite>.

Title: An associative model of Chinese university teachers' personality traits and students' classroom engagement from the teacher's perspective: the mediating role of emotional regulation
Snippet: This research contributed to filling the current theoretical gap regarding the relationship between teachers' personality traits and students' classroom engagement. Existing studies predominantly focused on factors such as classroom teaching methods and students' learning strategies, while lacking systematic exploration of the deeper connections between teachers' individual traits and student learning interactions (Qu and Wang, 2024). By incorporating the Big Five Personality Theory and emotional regulation theory, this study constructed a multidimensional theoretical framework to examine how teachers' personality traits predict students' classroom engagement from the teacher's perspective, offering a new perspective for enriching the theoretical system of educational psychology and pedagogy. The research also provided targeted guidance for professional development and classroom teaching improvement among university teachers. By uncovering the strengths and weaknesses of teachers with different personality traits in classroom management and instructional behaviors, this study offered a scientific basis for designing teacher training programs. Furthermore, by highlighting the critical role of emotional regulation in the teaching process, this research could help teachers enhance their emotional management abilities to better address complex challenges in teaching contexts. Ultimately, such practical guidance contributed to improving the quality of university classroom teaching and promoting comprehensive improvements in students' learning outcomes. 

Despite numerous studies examining the effects of teachers' personality traits (e.g., Extraversion, Conscientiousness) on students' classroom engagement and the role of emotional regulation in teaching contexts (Izydorczyk et al., 2025;Qu and Wang, 2024;Holl et al., 2024;Ilana, 2024;Zitzmann et al., 2024;Shdaifat et al., 2024), two gaps remain: 

Prior research has often focused on the direct relationship between a single personality dimension and classroom engagement, without systematically assessing the joint mechanisms and interactions of all five personality factors. To address this, our study is the first to employ the full NEO-PI-R five-factor framework to construct a "Teacher Personality-Emotional Regulation-Student Engagement" triadic interaction model, thereby revealing the distinct pathways and strengths of each dimension's effect on classroom engagement. 

Although some studies have suggested that emotional regulation may serve as a mediator of teaching effectiveness, this research has largely been confined to primary or secondary school settings, with a lack of empirical validation in higher education.

Title: Teacher Personality Predicts Emotional Well-Being and Academic Achievement in Students with Specific Learning Disorders
Snippet: While much of the literature has focused on the instructional or relational roles teachers play, emerging research highlights the importance of teacher personality in shaping students' school experiences. Personality theory, particularly the Five-Factor Model, offers a valuable framework for understanding how individual differences among teachers may influence educational processes [23]. In particular, traits such as conscientiousness, emotional stability, and extraversion are identified as especially relevant for effective teaching, with conscientiousness supporting structured and goal-oriented classroom management, emotional stability helping teachers manage negative emotions, and extraversion contributing to classroom engagement and positive teacher-student interactions [23]. 

Meta-analytic evidence underscores the relevance of teacher personality in relation to teacher effectiveness, a construct closely tied to classroom organization, instructional quality, and professional competence [24]. Among the Big Five traits, extraversion demonstrates the strongest overall association with teacher effectiveness, followed by conscientiousness, emotional stability, and openness. These traits are consistently linked to positive teaching behaviors across multiple rating sources. Agreeableness, in contrast, is not significantly associated with teacher effectiveness; it is also not consistently linked to key instructional or classroom outcomes across studies [24]. In addition, researchers have found that teachers with a "well-adjusted" personality profile, characterized by high conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and openness, and low neuroticism, report greater self-efficacy, engagement with students, and job satisfaction [25]. These qualities may help foster emotionally supportive and structured classrooms that are particularly beneficial for students with SLDs. Indeed, research has shown that teacher self-efficacy plays a central role in shaping instructional quality, classroom climate, and student academic adjustment [26].

Lastly, we examine whether teacher personality is important in different ways across educational levels (i.e., teachers teaching in elementary, secondary, and tertiary education). Poropat's (2009) hypothesis on the reduced influence of student personality on academic achievement due to increased variety of learning environments and activities with increasing levels of education can also be applied in the teacher context. That is, at lower educational levels, teacher personality has a greater influence on a variety of outcomes, given the comparably limited sources of learning students may have. Furthermore, teachers may have more opportunities to give individual attention and foster student engagement, often as a result of smaller classes at lower education levels (Blatchford et al. 2011). Finally, the greater emphasis on delivering a centralized and structured curriculum at higher levels of education, that often requires self-directed learning (Wilcox 1996), may diminish the opportunity for teacher personality to be displayed in teaching. This difference may explain how teacher emotional stability predicted student performance self-efficacy in secondary school students (Kim et al. 2018) but not in tertiary education students (Kim and MacCann 2018). The effect of these three phenomena is that there are more opportunities for a teacher's personality to be displayed and to be an influence to students. Thus, we expect that the association between teacher Big Five domains and the outcomes to be the strongest in lower educational levels (H5).
